title: TalkFlow: Structured Latent Flow Matching for Speech Driven Holistic Motion Generation
summary: Holistic co-speech motion generation aims to synthesize coordinated facial expressions, hand gestures, and body movements from speech, which is challenging due to heterogeneous part-specific dynamics, long-range temporal coherence, and cross-part coordination. Directly modeling high-dimensional motion can be unstable, while overly compact or unstructured latent spaces may lose fine-grained motion details. We present \textbf{TalkFlow}, a structured latent flow framework for speech-driven holistic motion generation. TalkFlow learns a continuous three-stream latent representation for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions, preserving part-specific dynamics without forcing heterogeneous motion components into a single latent space. To maintain holistic coordination, lightweight cross-stream interactions are incorporated in both latent representation learning and flow-based generation. Conditioned on multi-level speech features, TalkFlow performs speech-conditioned latent flow matching, learning a continuous transport process from source latents to realistic motion latents. Experiments on the BEAT2 dataset demonstrate strong performance across facial expression accuracy, body gesture quality, and speech-motion synchronization. Qualitative comparisons and user studies further show that TalkFlow generates more natural, expressive, and speech-aligned holistic motion than state-of-the-art methods. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TalkFlow generates speech-driven holistic motion (face, hands and body) with a structured latent flow matching model that keeps upper-body, lower-body and facial motion in separate latent streams linked by lightweight cross-stream interactions. Experiments on BEAT2 report strong facial accuracy, gesture quality and speech-motion synchronization.
AI.motivation: Co-speech holistic motion generation must coordinate heterogeneous part-specific dynamics and long-range coherence. Directly modeling high-dimensional motion is unstable, while compact or unstructured latent spaces lose fine-grained detail.
AI.method: A continuous three-stream latent representation for upper-body motion, lower-body motion and facial expressions, with cross-stream interactions in both latent learning and flow-based generation. Speech-conditioned latent flow matching, conditioned on multi-level speech features, transports source latents to realistic motion latents.
AI.result: On BEAT2, the method shows strong performance on facial expression accuracy, body gesture quality and speech-motion synchronization. Qualitative comparisons and user studies rate its motion as more natural, expressive and speech-aligned than state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Separating part-specific latent streams with light coupling offers a practical way to keep fine motion detail while preserving holistic coordination in speech-driven generation.

title: Dynamic Skinning: Kinematics-Driven Cartoon Effects for Articulated Characters
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures. Author's accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG), 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: We present an extension to traditional rig skinning, like Linear Blend Skinning (LBS), to produce secondary motions that exhibit the appearance of physical phenomena without need for simulation. At the core of the technique, we call dynamic skinning, is a set of deformers which offset position of individual vertices as a function of position derivatives and time. Examples of such deformers create effects such as oscillation in response to movement and the appearance of wave propagation, among others. Because the technique computes offsets directly and does not solve physics equations, it is extremely fast to compute. It also boasts a high degree of customizability which supports a desirable artist workflow and fine level of control. Finally, we showcase the technique in a number of scenarios and make comparisons with the state of the art.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Skinning extends rig skinning such as Linear Blend Skinning with deformers that offset vertex positions from position derivatives and time, producing secondary motion effects like oscillation and wave propagation without physics simulation.
AI.motivation: Secondary motion in articulated characters usually needs physical simulation, which is costly and hard to control for artists.
AI.method: A set of deformers that compute per-vertex position offsets as functions of position derivatives and time, added on top of standard skinning. The offsets are computed directly rather than by solving physics equations, and the deformers are customizable.
AI.result: The abstract reports the technique is extremely fast to compute and showcases it in several scenarios with comparisons to the state of the art. It gives no quantitative figures in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a fast, artist-controllable alternative to simulation for cartoon-style secondary motion in rigged characters.

title: SemEllipsoid: Semantic-aware Shape Abstraction with Ellipsoid
summary: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.

AI.tldr: SemEllipsoid introduces semantic-aware shape abstraction, which approximates a 3D shape with ellipsoidal primitives that each lie within a single semantic part. It is non-learning-based and uses semantic cues from large foundation models.
AI.motivation: Geometry-aware shape abstraction preserves shape fidelity but often lets primitives span multiple semantic parts, which causes artifacts in part-level editing and manipulation.
AI.method: Semantic constraints are injected into primitive optimization. A fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme measures semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and an alternating optimization iteratively solves for semantic assignment and primitive configuration. The method needs no data collection or network training and supports multiple abstraction levels.
AI.result: The abstract reports extensive experiments across several 3D shape collections that validate effectiveness and generalization to shapes from arbitrary categories. It gives no quantitative figures in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Semantic consistency can be added to shape abstraction without learning, which makes primitive-based representations more usable for part-level shape editing.

title: Altered Visual Hand Feedback in Virtual Reality: An Exploratory Study in Essential Tremor
summary: Pathological tremor is the most prevalent movement disorder worldwide, characterized by involuntary muscular oscillations within a frequency of 3 to 12 Hz. Despite extensive research, the underlying mechanisms that generate and modulate tremor are not yet understood, and treatments are usually insufficient. While it is known that visual feedback is an important afferent pathway, little is known about the impact of altering the hand's visual representation on tremor expression. With the development of immersive technologies, VR poses an excellent tool to study how alterations to the representation of the hands affect tremor. In this work, we study this through two complementary experiments. In the first one, we show that a consumer-level hand-tracking system substantially attenuates tremor-band movements without preventing successful task completion. In the second one, with eight patients with essential tremor, we observe task-dependent differences in physical tremor between VR and the real world, with several patients exhibiting lower tremor-band activity in both hand kinematics and muscle oscillations, particularly during reaching tasks. Our findings represent an initial step toward validating the use of VR as an experimental tool for the research and treatment of pathological tremor, while highlighting strong user- and task-dependent effects.

AI.tldr: An exploratory study in essential tremor compares tremor-band movement in VR with the real world, showing that a consumer hand-tracking system attenuates tremor-band movement and that patients show task-dependent tremor differences between VR and reality.
AI.motivation: The mechanisms that generate and modulate pathological tremor are not well understood, treatments are often insufficient, and it is unknown how altering the visual representation of the hand affects tremor.
AI.method: Two complementary experiments. The first tests whether a consumer-level hand-tracking system changes tremor-band movement while the task is still completed. The second records eight patients with essential tremor in VR and in the real world and compares hand kinematics and muscle oscillations.
AI.result: Hand tracking substantially attenuates tremor-band movement without preventing task completion. Several of the eight patients show lower tremor-band activity in VR in both hand kinematics and muscle oscillations, especially during reaching tasks, and effects depend on user and task.
AI.conclusion: The results are an initial step toward validating VR as an experimental tool for research and treatment of pathological tremor, with strong user- and task-dependent effects that need further study.

title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
summary: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper uses large language models to automatically construct simple baselines for 36 deep learning tasks from Nature, Science and Cell-family papers. The automatically built baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5 percent of the gap between a trivial predictor and the deep learning model.
AI.motivation: Many apparent gains in deep learning for physical and life sciences disappear when appropriate baselines are included, and human peer review struggles to keep up with the volume of papers.
AI.method: Thirty-six supervised classification and regression tasks are assembled from peer-reviewed studies. A language model constructs a simple baseline for each task, and the authors vary test-time compute and the level of study context given to the model.
AI.result: The median automatically built baseline matches or exceeds the deep learning model in 12 studies. Mean gap recovery is 85.7 percent, and the paper also reports variation across scientific domains and publication venues.
AI.conclusion: Automated baseline construction looks like a practical and scalable check on deep learning claims in the physical and life sciences.

title: Bayesian Distribution System State Estimation with Flow Matching
summary: Medium-voltage feeders have few real-time measurements, so distribution system state estimation (DSSE) rests on pseudo-measurements of the secondary substations, a prior in Bayesian terms. Weighted least squares keeps the power flow exact but reduces this prior to a mean and variance, while supervised deep learning estimators also learn the power flow and are tied to one measurement set. We propose PoSE (posterior sampling for state estimation), which keeps the Bayesian structure of DSSE and learns only what the distribution system operator does not know, namely the distribution of substation injections, modelled by a neural network trained with flow matching on historical data. The power flow equations, grid topology and measurements enter only at sampling, through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction. The neural network therefore never approximates the power flow, but every posterior sample is a physically consistent operating point, and one trained prior serves any measurement set, noise level and topology. On the IEEE 33-bus feeder, PoSE lowers the probabilistic injection error (CRPS) by 6.7-7.5% against a full-covariance Gaussian prior in all 12 tested settings. It provides reliable uncertainty: the 90% intervals contain the true injection almost exactly as often as exact posterior samples would, whereas those of supervised estimators contain it in only 37-78% of cases. On the 240-bus unbalanced three-phase Iowa feeder, it gives the lowest injection, voltage and branch-current errors of all estimators. A fast variant matches this accuracy at 0.2-0.6s per snapshot and, without retraining, beats Gaussian priors and retrained supervised estimators on seven reconfigured topologies.

AI.tldr: PoSE performs Bayesian distribution system state estimation by learning only the distribution of substation injections with a flow-matching prior. The power flow, topology and measurements are applied only at sampling through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction, so every posterior sample is physically consistent.
AI.motivation: Medium-voltage feeders have few real-time measurements. Weighted least squares reduces the prior to a mean and variance, and supervised deep learning estimators are tied to a single measurement set.
AI.method: A neural prior trained with flow matching on historical data models substation injections. Power flow equations, grid topology and measurements enter only during posterior sampling through a noise-aware Kalman-type correction, so the network never approximates the power flow. One trained prior serves any measurement set, noise level and topology.
AI.result: On the IEEE 33-bus feeder, CRPS for injection error falls 6.7 to 7.5 percent against a full-covariance Gaussian prior in all 12 tested settings. The 90 percent intervals cover the true injection about as often as exact posterior samples would, while supervised estimators cover it in only 37 to 78 percent of cases. On a 240-bus unbalanced three-phase Iowa feeder it gives the lowest injection, voltage and branch-current errors. A fast variant runs at 0.2 to 0.6 s per snapshot and beats Gaussian priors and retrained supervised estimators on seven reconfigured topologies without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Learning the operator's unknown injection distribution while keeping the physics in the sampling step yields reliable uncertainty and transfers across measurement sets and topologies.

title: Don't Just Impute, Detect: Task-Aware Diffusion Pipelines for Edge Anomaly Detection
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 33rd IEEE International Conference on High Performance Computing, Data, and Analytics (HiPC 2026)
summary: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge pipelines routinely lose contiguous blocks of multi-sensor data to network dropouts and hardware faults. The standard remedy is a disjointed "impute-then-detect" pipeline whose imputer is trained only for Mean Squared Error (MSE). Such an imputer fills a missing block with the most probable normal pattern: a partially observed anomaly is smoothed back toward normality, and boundary artifacts on normal data raise false alarms. We call this imputation bias and propose the Task-Aware Diffusion Refiner (TADR), a conditional diffusion refiner trained against the loss landscape of a frozen downstream detector. Because back-propagating through the sampling trajectory is intractable, the task-aware terms act on the one-step clean-window estimate that the noise prediction already yields, so training costs no more than plain diffusion training. Under strict Point-to-Point evaluation over five seeds with paired significance tests, TADR raises F1 by $0.338$ over the unrefined detector on SMD ($p = 0.0015$), and the anomaly enhancement objective alone contributes $0.463$ in ablation. We also characterise when the method helps: the gain tracks the continuous, mutually redundant channels available and the anomaly evidence the outage removes, and it is absent on telemetry datasets dominated by one-hot command channels and on PSM. At ten sampling steps TADR runs in $41.4$ ms per window on a single CPU core, sustaining about $24$ concurrent 1 Hz streams from a $4.03$ MB model. Code and per-seed results are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TADR is a conditional diffusion refiner for edge anomaly detection that is trained against the loss of a frozen downstream detector, instead of imputing missing sensor blocks with an MSE-only imputer. On SMD it raises F1 by 0.338 over the unrefined detector and runs in 41.4 ms per window on one CPU core.
AI.motivation: Impute-then-detect pipelines use imputers trained only for MSE, which fill missing blocks with the most probable normal pattern. This smooths partially observed anomalies toward normality and creates boundary artifacts that raise false alarms.
AI.method: A task-aware diffusion refiner trained against the loss landscape of a frozen detector. Because backpropagation through the sampling trajectory is intractable, the task-aware terms act on the one-step clean-window estimate that the noise prediction already yields, so training costs the same as plain diffusion training.
AI.result: Under strict point-to-point evaluation over five seeds with paired significance tests, F1 rises by 0.338 on SMD (p = 0.0015), and the anomaly enhancement objective alone contributes 0.463 in ablation. The gain is absent on telemetry datasets dominated by one-hot command channels and on PSM. At ten sampling steps the method runs at 41.4 ms per window on a single CPU core, sustaining about 24 concurrent 1 Hz streams from a 4.03 MB model.
AI.conclusion: Training the imputer for the downstream detection objective helps when continuous, redundant channels are available, and the authors also characterise when it does not help.

title: Unsupervised Feature Selection Using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality -- Extended Version
comment: Preprint submitted to Elsevier Pattern Recognition
summary: High dimensionality degrades both the efficiency and the effectiveness of learning algorithms, and in many applications no class labels are available to guide dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes LIDFS, an unsupervised feature selection method based on Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID). The method builds on the formal equivalence between LID and the indiscriminability of distance measures. The data matrix is transposed so that each feature is treated as a point, and the LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from the distances to its $k$ nearest neighboring features. Features with lower LID exhibit greater local discriminability and receive higher importance scores. A refinement step then retains one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The result is a complete ranking from which any number of features can be selected without rerunning the procedure. LIDFS does not use any information about labels or the number of classes, and runs in $\mathcal{O}(d^2 n)$ time for $n$ instances and $d$ features. LIDFS is compared with classic and state-of-the-art methods and a random baseline on 23 high-dimensional datasets, the classic benchmark collection. The evaluation uses classification accuracy and AUC with five downstream classifiers, as well as clustering accuracy and normalized mutual information, over both full and aggressive selection ranges. LIDFS ranks first in the supervised evaluations and first or tied second in the clustering-based evaluations. It belongs to the top statistical group together with methods that require the number of classes, and it runs faster than its closest competitor. Several recent methods, by contrast, fail to outperform the random baseline. A sensitivity analysis shows that small neighborhood sizes yield the best results.

AI.tldr: LIDFS is an unsupervised feature selection method that ranks features by their local intrinsic dimensionality, estimated per feature from its k nearest neighboring features, and produces a complete ranking that needs no labels or class count.
AI.motivation: High dimensionality hurts both the efficiency and effectiveness of learning, and many applications have no class labels to guide dimensionality reduction.
AI.method: The data matrix is transposed so each feature is a point. The LID of each feature is estimated by maximum likelihood from distances to its k nearest neighboring features, and lower LID gives higher importance. A refinement step keeps one representative per feature neighborhood and demotes locally redundant features. The runtime is O(d^2 n) for n instances and d features.
AI.result: On 23 high-dimensional datasets, LIDFS ranks first in supervised evaluations (classification accuracy and AUC with five classifiers) and first or tied second in clustering evaluations (accuracy and NMI). It is in the top statistical group with methods that require the number of classes, runs faster than its closest competitor, and several recent methods fail to beat a random baseline. Small neighborhood sizes give the best results.
AI.conclusion: A label-free, LID-based ranking is competitive with the best methods, including those that use class information, and is efficient.

title: Certified Behavioral Retention for Continual Adaptation with Held-Out Anchors
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents (CL4M / CL4FMAgents)
summary: Continual adaptation requires deciding not only how to update a model, but whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior. We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance. CABA provides an auditable retention check for candidate generators exposing comparable policy distributions and a declared update path, while deployment also requires separate evidence of current-task utility.

AI.tldr: CABA is a post-update gate for continual adaptation that accepts a candidate update only if its worst-anchor forward KL divergence on held-out historical anchors stays within a declared budget. It reduces forgetting to 0.00 percent on a UCI Human Activity Recognition proxy at the cost of some accuracy.
AI.motivation: Continual adaptation needs a way to decide whether to commit an update without exceeding a declared budget for changes to protected behavior.
AI.method: Historical observations are reserved from candidate optimization. Old and candidate policies are compared on frozen representations, and the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL stays within budget is selected. The check needs neither action labels nor complete trajectories. Theory gives uniform behavioral-divergence bounds on protected support under representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions.
AI.result: On a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study, mean forgetting falls from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at epsilon = 0.05, while final average accuracy drops from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance.
AI.conclusion: CABA gives an auditable retention check for candidate generators with comparable policy distributions, and deployment still needs separate evidence of current-task utility.

title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
summary: Humans and animals have a unique capacity to generalize and learn in novel circumstances, including "0-shot" inference (ZI) and continual learning (CL) -- two powerful cognitive abilities. Despite this importance, efforts to model ZI and CL are seriously limited in several ways. First, existing models typically lack components critical to ZI and CL in the brain, namely, strong inductive biases (for ZI) and autonomous control of learning (for CL). Second, models can be less tractable to analysis if model components are overly complex (lacking simplicity), or too task-restricted if model components are overly bespoke (lacking expressivity). Here we introduce autonomous Hebbian networks ("AutoHebb"), a class of online learning feedforward neural networks that realize strong inductive biases and autonomously controlled learning, and are both simple and expressive. Unlike standard models that learn via externally controlled optimization (e.g. gradient descent), AutoHebb networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal ('neuromodulator') fed back to the network. The neuromodulator in turn gates a biologically grounded local learning rule (3-factor Hebbian rule) that updates networks' plastic weights. Using meta-learning to search for fixed (non-plastic) weights, we find that AutoHebb networks (1) succeed on ZI tasks, (2) show emergent (untrained) ZI/CL abilities, (3) admit reverse-engineering into explicit algorithms, and (4) outperform modern learning models on ZI/CL tasks. Lastly, performance comparisons to related models implied an essential role for three model components: meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity, and autonomous control of learning. These findings indicate that AutoHebb may be useful in hypothesis generation, analysis, and discovery of biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.

AI.tldr: AutoHebb is a class of online feedforward networks in which a global neuromodulator, built from external feedback and internal activity, gates a three-factor Hebbian learning rule. Meta-learned fixed weights let it perform zero-shot inference and continual learning, and it outperforms modern learning models on these tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing computational models of zero-shot inference and continual learning lack the strong inductive biases and autonomous control of learning seen in the brain, and they are often either too complex to analyze or too task-specific.
AI.method: Autonomous Hebbian networks combine external feedback with internally generated activity to produce a global learning signal that gates a biologically grounded local learning rule. Meta-learning searches for fixed, non-plastic weights.
AI.result: AutoHebb networks succeed on zero-shot inference tasks, show emergent untrained ZI and CL abilities, can be reverse-engineered into explicit algorithms, and outperform modern learning models on ZI and CL tasks. Comparisons suggest that meta-learning, Hebbian plasticity and autonomous control of learning are each essential.
AI.conclusion: AutoHebb may help generate hypotheses and discover biologically grounded forms of learning and generalization.

title: Frozen in Time: How a Physics Foundation Model Forgets Under Sim-to-Real Adaptation
comment: Accepted at the Sim2Science workshop, NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Scientific foundation models (SciFMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of PDEs, including the ability to efficiently adapt to unseen data distributions with additional finetuning. As with all neural architectures, finetuning such models comes with the risk of catastrophic forgetting, whereby adapting to new tasks degrades prior knowledge of the model. We study catastrophic forgetting in Walrus-1.3B, a SciFM for continuum dynamics, over the course of a two-stage sim-to-real adaptation: first finetuning on simulated flow around a cylinder and then adapting to experimental data of the same system. We find that finetuning on the simulations rapidly degrades rollout performance on the original pretraining datasets, with one-step errors increasing up to 35x after just 20 epochs. Subsequent adaptation to real data further erodes performance on the simulated task. We characterize the potential drivers of forgetting, such as dataset dependence and task representation similarity. We then show that replaying as little as 1% simulated data during real-data finetuning recovers most of the lost simulation performance while retaining effective adaptation to the experimental dynamics. Our results identify catastrophic forgetting as a practical obstacle to sim-to-real adaptation of SciFMs and show that lightweight replay strategies significantly improve retention.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning the physics foundation model Walrus-1.3B on simulated flow around a cylinder and then on experimental data causes catastrophic forgetting of its pretraining datasets. Replaying as little as 1 percent of simulated data during real-data fine-tuning recovers most of the lost simulation performance.
AI.motivation: Scientific foundation models can adapt efficiently to new distributions, but fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting, and the sim-to-real adaptation of such models is not well understood.
AI.method: Two-stage sim-to-real adaptation of Walrus-1.3B for continuum dynamics: first fine-tuning on simulated flow around a cylinder, then adaptation to experimental data of the same system. The authors characterise drivers of forgetting such as dataset dependence and task representation similarity, and test replay of simulated data during the real-data stage.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on simulations quickly degrades rollout performance on the original pretraining datasets, with one-step errors rising up to 35 times after 20 epochs. Adaptation to real data further erodes performance on the simulated task. Replaying 1 percent of simulated data recovers most of the lost simulation performance while still adapting to experimental dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting is a practical obstacle to sim-to-real adaptation of scientific foundation models, and lightweight replay significantly improves retention.

title: FARO: Function-Space Adaptive Return-to-Risk Optimization via Cross-Block Equal-Risk-Contribution Budget Allocation
summary: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FARO is a function-space adaptive optimizer for LLM training that assigns each parameter block its own geometry from realized counterfactual return and reallocates a shared update budget across blocks by equal risk contribution. On a GPT-style model on FineWeb it matches the best hand-designed recipe and improves on it modestly.
AI.motivation: LLM training splits work between optimizers by hand, with orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices and Adam-style updates elsewhere. This rests on human priors and fixes one global update budget shared by all blocks.
AI.method: Parameter blocks are the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry based on its realized counterfactual return, freezes the routes, and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution, the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory.
AI.result: The FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam at 3.2794. FARO-ERC lowers clean-data loss at all 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, with sign test, paired test and confidence interval agreeing. The gain exceeds run-to-run noise at no added time or memory and holds under a corrupted data stream.
AI.conclusion: The framework recovers the human prior without hand-set per-layer geometry, and its equal-risk reallocation gives a modest but robust improvement by trimming the riskiest blocks.

title: Near-Optimal First-Order Regret for Bandits with Feedback Graphs
summary: We study first-order regret guarantees for adversarial bandits with a fixed, known directed feedback graph. For strongly observable graphs, [ACBDK15] establishes a minimax regret of $\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{\alpha T})$, where $\alpha$ denotes the independence number of the graph and $T$ denotes the horizon. On the other hand, the best existing first-order bound scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{(\kappa+1) L^\star})$ [LLZ20], where $\kappa$ denotes the clique partition number, satisfying $\kappa+1\geq\alpha$, and $L^\star$ denotes the cumulative loss of the best arm, leaving a gap between the graph dependence in worst-case and first-order guarantees. In this paper, we bridge this gap by obtaining an expected regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\alpha L^\star}+\alpha)$. Our first result is an algorithm for the special case of self-aware graphs, in which every vertex has a self-loop. The algorithm combines the update of EXP3 [ACBFS02] with a sampling rule inspired by exploration by optimization [LS20]. More specifically, we construct a map whose fixed points yield sampling distributions that control the one-round regret remainder in terms of the learner's loss and the graph's independence number, which is crucial in deriving optimal first-order guarantees. We further show that a sufficiently accurate fixed point can be computed in polynomial time by a geometrically convergent iteration. Finally, we extend the algorithm to general strongly observable graphs and achieve the same $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\alpha L^\star}+\alpha)$ guarantee by adapting the two-level aggregation approach of [LLZ20].

AI.tldr: The paper proves an expected regret bound of O~(sqrt(alpha L*) + alpha) for adversarial bandits with a known directed feedback graph, where alpha is the independence number and L* the best arm's cumulative loss. This closes a gap between worst-case and first-order graph dependence.
AI.motivation: For strongly observable graphs the minimax regret scales with sqrt(alpha T), but the best first-order bound depends on the clique partition number kappa, which can be much larger than alpha.
AI.method: For self-aware graphs, where every vertex has a self-loop, the algorithm combines the EXP3 update with a sampling rule inspired by exploration by optimization. Sampling distributions are fixed points of a constructed map that controls the one-round regret remainder, and a sufficiently accurate fixed point is computed in polynomial time by a geometrically convergent iteration. The method extends to general strongly observable graphs using two-level aggregation from prior work.
AI.result: The abstract claims the bound O~(sqrt(alpha L*) + alpha) in expectation for both self-aware and general strongly observable graphs. It gives no empirical results.
AI.conclusion: The first-order regret bound matches the graph-dependent worst-case rate through alpha, which makes it the near-optimal first-order guarantee for these bandit settings.

title: TensorSSM: Memorizing Spatial Position in Dynamic State Space for Tensor Core Generation
summary: High-dimensional tensors are ubiquitous in real-world applications but lead to massive storage overhead. Functional tensor decomposition addresses this by employing neural networks to map element coordinates to tensor cores, significantly reducing the parameters for data compression. However, existing functional methods typically flatten high-order tensors into 1D sequences. This folding operation causes highly overlapping local coordinate sequences and struggles to capture complex cross-mode spatial dependencies, severely limiting their expressiveness on diverse datasets. To tackle these challenges, we propose TensorSSM, a novel Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for functional decomposition method that memorizes spatial positions within a dynamic State Space Model (SSM). Specifically, TensorSSM first decomposes mode-wise coordinates into sequences spit by K-ary rule, encoding spatial tokens from coarse to fine, which effectively captures spatial variations. Furthermore, we extend the SSM's state space to explicitly map cross-mode spatial dependencies, allowing inter-mode interactions to enhance the updates of each mode. By integrating cross-mode information from previous hidden states into the current state transitions, TensorSSM effectively expands tensor representation along two dimensions: the sequence dimension for coarse-to-fine spatial tokens, and the state dimension for cross-mode memorization. This design effectively integrates spatial information into the state space and the tensor core, substantially advancing the state adaptability and enhancing the expressiveness of the data compression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TensorSSM achieves significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, exhibiting robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without relying on strict spatial assumptions.

AI.tldr: TensorSSM is an implicit neural representation for functional tensor decomposition that uses a dynamic state space model to memorize spatial positions. It encodes mode-wise coordinates as coarse-to-fine tokens and adds cross-mode dependencies to the state, improving reconstruction and storage efficiency.
AI.motivation: Functional tensor methods flatten high-order tensors into 1D coordinate sequences, which overlap heavily locally and struggle to capture cross-mode spatial dependencies, limiting expressiveness on diverse datasets.
AI.method: Mode-wise coordinates are split into sequences by a K-ary rule and encoded from coarse to fine. The state space is extended to map cross-mode dependencies, so inter-mode information from previous hidden states feeds the current state transition. The sequence dimension carries spatial tokens and the state dimension carries cross-mode memory.
AI.result: The abstract reports significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, with robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without strict spatial assumptions. It names no specific datasets or numbers in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Integrating spatial information into the state space and tensor core improves the expressiveness of functional tensor compression.

title: TSFLab: A Self-Improving Agent-Agnostic Workbench for Time Series Forecasting Research
summary: As publications and products on time series forecasting (TSF) proliferate, researchers face a growing burden of analyzing existing work. First, not all publications release code. For instance, only about 20% of arXiv TSF papers have a code link in the surveyed period. Second, released code also requires manual maintenance. Thus, TSF researchers must constantly adapt or implement existing works. However, independent implementations can differ in experimental settings and are difficult to maintain. We therefore propose to use AI agents for benchmarking TSF research and even supporting autoresearch, e.g., developing new TSF models. Yet directly applying existing coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, is suboptimal: prohibitive costs, limited scalability to large research projects (e.g., benchmarking), and lack of self-maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose TSFLab, a self-improving agent-agnostic "workbench" that equips compatible coding agents with shared resources and tools for low-cost TSF research and continuous maintenance of research resources. Our experiments cover reproduction, benchmarking, and new method development. In reproduction and benchmarking, TSFLab improves task completion by 20-163% and cuts fresh tokens per completed task by 11-66% across baselines. A pilot study of agent-driven method development also shows improved forecasting accuracy via TSFLab, with 32.8-73.6% fewer fresh tokens and 9.2-68.8% less development time than the other settings.

AI.tldr: TSFLab is an agent-agnostic workbench that gives coding agents shared resources and tools for low-cost time series forecasting research, including reproduction, benchmarking, method development and self-maintenance. It improves task completion by 20 to 163 percent and cuts fresh tokens per completed task by 11 to 66 percent in reproduction and benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Only about 20 percent of arXiv time series forecasting papers have a code link in the surveyed period, released code needs maintenance, and independent implementations differ in settings. Existing coding agents are costly, scale poorly to large benchmarking projects and do not maintain themselves.
AI.method: A self-improving workbench equips compatible coding agents with shared resources and tools for low-cost research and continuous maintenance of research resources. Experiments cover reproduction, benchmarking and new method development.
AI.result: In reproduction and benchmarking, task completion improves by 20 to 163 percent and fresh tokens per completed task fall by 11 to 66 percent across baselines. A pilot study of agent-driven method development shows better forecasting accuracy with 32.8 to 73.6 percent fewer fresh tokens and 9.2 to 68.8 percent less development time.
AI.conclusion: Shared, self-maintaining resources make AI agents a practical tool for benchmarking and developing time series forecasting methods.

title: No Channels Left Behind: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration through Residual Gates
summary: Training acceleration methods for diffusion transformers, such as REPA and dispersive regularization, are commonly explained by additional supervision, spatial-structure priors, or improved feature geometry. We revisit this view and uncover a striking internal change: the AdaLN-Zero residual gate $\alpha$, which directly controls how conditioned updates enter the residual stream, is substantially reorganized by these methods. This observation motivates our hypothesis that acceleration arises, at least in part, from reshaping the residual gating pathway rather than solely from the feature structures explicitly imposed by auxiliary objectives. Supporting this view, accelerated models are markedly more sensitive to perturbations of $\alpha$, and their gate geometry reflects semantic relationships among classes. We further introduce the normalized participation ratio (nPR) to characterize the channel-wise organization of the gates and find that, across REPA teachers, projector architectures, and radial-objective targets, broader gate participation accompanies better generation quality. Guided by this insight, we propose a simple teacher-free radial objective that promotes broader gate participation through feature-norm regularization, without pairwise feature comparisons. On ImageNet $256\times256$ with SiT-B/2, our method improves FID over dispersive loss while increasing mean gate participation over timesteps and classes, further supporting the link between gate organization and training acceleration. Our results identify residual-gate reorganization as a measurable axis of diffusion training acceleration and suggest a simple direction for further acceleration.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that training-acceleration methods for diffusion transformers such as REPA and dispersive regularization reorganize the AdaLN-Zero residual gate. It proposes a teacher-free radial objective that broadens gate participation through feature-norm regularization and improves FID over dispersive loss on ImageNet 256 with SiT-B/2.
AI.motivation: Acceleration of diffusion transformer training is usually explained by extra supervision, spatial priors or better feature geometry. The authors test whether the residual gating pathway itself drives acceleration.
AI.method: The authors measure the AdaLN-Zero gate alpha across methods, test its sensitivity to perturbations, and introduce the normalized participation ratio to describe channel-wise gate organization. They then propose a radial objective that uses feature-norm regularization and avoids pairwise feature comparisons.
AI.result: Across REPA teachers, projector architectures and radial-objective targets, broader gate participation goes with better generation quality. On ImageNet 256 with SiT-B/2, the proposed method improves FID over dispersive loss while increasing mean gate participation over timesteps and classes.
AI.conclusion: Residual-gate reorganization is a measurable axis of diffusion training acceleration and points to a simple route for further speed-ups.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding and Building "Any-task inference" Capable Foundation Models
summary: In this work, we provide a formal framework and mathematical definition for the subset of foundation models focused on enabling the property of "any-task inference" (ATI) (similar to zero-shot inference), rather than those designed for pre-training fine-tuning. To achieve this mathematical definition, we formalize the notion of a "space of tasks of interest," which we include in the problem domain, then provide an interface-based formal definition for ATI foundation models as those that map samples of data $x$ and tasks $t$ to predictions over the space of labels directly. While simple, this definition allows us to show that all ATI foundation models can be decomposed through a "universal task reduction" lens into encoder, model, and decoder aspects. We can leverage this decomposition to also decompose foundation model error into terms corresponding to different aspects of this reduction, stratified into a collection of "design terms," which are theoretical properties that can inform one of whether a particular proposed ATI foundation model can achieve optimality or not due to the structure of the proposed task reduction, and "realized model excess" terms which capture interactions between learned and programmatic components of foundation model systems. Lastly, we can use this perspective to offer two "prototypical" recipes for realizing ATI foundation models in diverse domains, which we term generative and discriminative variants of ATI foundation models. This exercise is grounded throughout by 5 real-world examples of foundation models in different settings, varying greatly in how these capabilities are realized, showing the applicability of this definition to real-world settings.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a formal definition of any-task inference (ATI) foundation models, which map data and tasks directly to label predictions. It shows that all such models decompose into encoder, model and decoder aspects through universal task reduction, and it offers generative and discriminative recipes for building them.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are often defined by pretraining and fine-tuning, but the subset that enables zero-shot style inference on arbitrary tasks lacks a formal treatment that explains its error and design requirements.
AI.method: The authors formalise a space of tasks of interest and define ATI models as interfaces from data and tasks to label predictions. A universal task reduction lens decomposes the model into encoder, model and decoder parts, and the error is split into design terms and realized model excess terms. Two prototypical recipes are given, generative and discriminative.
AI.result: The framework is illustrated with five real-world foundation models in different settings. The abstract reports no quantitative experiments.
AI.conclusion: The decomposition gives a common language for designing and analysing ATI foundation models, with design terms indicating whether a proposed reduction can reach optimality.

title: Fair Recommender Systems for Intersecting Groups
summary: Recommendation systems that optimize for the average user can fail to capture the preferences of diverse demographic groups. We consider a dynamic recommendation system, where arriving users can belong to different demographic groups. Importantly, these groups can intersect, and a user may belong to several groups. We first show that over time, any group-blind policy (which excludes all current-user group information) recommending $K \geq 1$ items incurs linear total regret under mild conditions. In turn, we introduce three group-aware algorithms based on the classical Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB): i) Intersection-Fitting, which runs UCB on each intersection, but has a sublinear group- and intersection-level regret guarantee with an exponential dependence in the number of groups; and ii) two group-level heuristics, Inner-Outer UCB and Group-Item UCB which allocate different arms to different groups, and use a sleeping expert meta-learner to choose which active group's recommendation an intersection should inherit at any given time step. We provide experimental results on two datasets, Goodreads and BoardGameGeek, and highlight that our heuristics can be preferable to the intersection-fitting algorithm when intersection-level preferences are closely related to group-level preferences, but that intersection-fitting performs better when different intersections within a same group prefer different items.

AI.tldr: The paper studies fair recommendation for users who belong to intersecting demographic groups. It shows that group-blind policies incur linear regret and proposes three group-aware UCB-based algorithms, evaluated on Goodreads and BoardGameGeek.
AI.motivation: A recommender that optimizes for the average user can miss the preferences of diverse demographic groups, and groups can overlap so that a user belongs to several of them.
AI.method: The authors first prove that any group-blind policy recommending K or more items incurs linear total regret under mild conditions. They then introduce Intersection-Fitting, which runs UCB on each intersection with sublinear group and intersection regret but exponential dependence on the number of groups, and two group-level heuristics, Inner-Outer UCB and Group-Item UCB, which use a sleeping-expert meta-learner to choose which group's recommendation an intersection inherits.
AI.result: On Goodreads and BoardGameGeek, the heuristics can beat Intersection-Fitting when intersection preferences closely follow group preferences, while Intersection-Fitting is better when different intersections within a group prefer different items.
AI.conclusion: The choice between intersection-level and group-level algorithms depends on how closely intersection preferences track group preferences.

title: Kernel-based Interpolatory Methods for Context Compression of Attention Mechanisms
summary: The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two KV-cache compression methods, GAIM and Q-DAIM, that treat attention as a ratio of linear maps in a kernel Hilbert space and select interpolation nodes with empirical interpolation. Taylor, Performer and Random Fourier Feature surrogates make compression run in linear time, and the methods extend to streaming attention.
AI.motivation: Attention cost is quadratic in context length, which makes KV-cache compression an important problem for modern language models.
AI.method: Attention is formulated in the Hilbert space of its kernel, where it is a ratio of two linear maps, so the linear maps themselves can be interpolated. GAIM and Q-DAIM build on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method. Surrogate models make the cost linear in context length, and streaming variants penalize reselection of earlier nodes and update past interpolations.
AI.result: Numerical results show convergence of the residuals and output error for future queries, and preliminary results on LongBench-E show performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The authors suggest the Q-DAIM range can locate where information concentrates in the KV cache.
AI.conclusion: Interpolation in the kernel Hilbert space offers an efficient route to KV-cache compression, with the Q-DAIM range as a possible diagnostic for information placement.

title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
summary: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the \textbf{training-inference mismatch} between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. \textit{We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.} Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a \textit{numerical discrepancy} of the engine and a \textit{policy lag} of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the \textbf{discrepancy-lag correction} (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.

AI.tldr: The paper traces training-inference mismatch in LLM reinforcement learning to two sources, engine numerical discrepancy and trainer policy lag, and proposes the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC). Under a stale sampler DLC keeps KL from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy runs on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B.
AI.motivation: Sampling by an inference engine with stale asynchronous weights makes the training data off-policy. A correction that stabilizes training under one mismatch source can fail under the other, so the authors ask which property of a source determines the needed correction.
AI.method: Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error into a numerical discrepancy of the engine and a policy lag of the trainer. DLC centers the numerical discrepancy at each prefix, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights, and resynchronizes the sampler when the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half.
AI.result: Importance weighting alone fails on Qwen3-1.7B once the effective sample size drops below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy runs on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B. Its resynchronization prevents collapses that per-token corrections leave and that a KL on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.
AI.conclusion: Policy lag is fed back by the trainer's own updates, so correcting it needs a feedback-aware method such as resynchronization rather than per-token weighting alone.

title: CAMEL: Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning for Ultra-Lightweight Retinal Foundation Models
summary: Recent progress in deep learning has substantially advanced automated grading of ophthalmologic pathologies, supported by large annotated datasets and improved representation learning. However, a significant gap remains between state-of-the-art performance and clinical scalability. In particular, foundation models have reshaped image-based medical screening and diagnosis. These large-scale architectures trained on extensive datasets learn rich, generalizable feature representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In ophthalmology, RETFound, one of the most relevant foundation models for retinal images, performs strongly across classification, segmentation, and risk prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, foundation models are often computationally prohibitive, hindering their deployment in real-world clinical environments where hardware constraints and latency are critical. To bridge this gap, we introduce CAMEL (Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning), a novel cross-architecture distillation framework that uses an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning to effectively transfer knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact, lightweight student models. Our experimental evaluation across four datasets shows that CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity, enabling lightweight yet highly accurate models suitable for resource-limited clinical settings.

AI.tldr: CAMEL is a cross-architecture distillation framework that uses asymmetric masked embedding learning to compress large retinal foundation models into ultra-lightweight student models that keep their accuracy.
AI.motivation: Retinal foundation models such as RETFound perform strongly on classification, segmentation and risk prediction, but they are computationally prohibitive for clinical deployment where hardware and latency are constrained.
AI.method: A cross-architecture distillation framework that transfers knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact student models, using an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning.
AI.result: Across four datasets CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity.
AI.conclusion: It produces lightweight yet highly accurate models suited to resource-limited clinical settings.

title: Monte Carlo Random Walk Kernel
summary: We introduce the Monte Carlo Random Walk Kernel (MCRWK), an estimator whose per-pair cost is independent of graph size and derived directly from the random walk kernel (RWK) expansion. By normalizing the kernel coefficients, MCRWK samples a shared walk length and estimates its contribution using random walks on the input graphs. This gives a simple way to approximate RWK without constructing the product graph. For a fixed expected walk length and efficient neighbor sampling, each pairwise estimate takes $O(m)$ time for $m$ Monte Carlo samples, allowing the sample budget to control the trade-off between runtime and accuracy. We evaluate MCRWK against Graph Voyagers and classical RWK methods on synthetic and real graph datasets. In the reported experiments on large synthetic graphs, MCRWK is faster than Graph Voyagers and, at matched runtime, more accurate. It also has the lowest Gram-matrix runtime on the five real datasets studied. Code and experiments are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: MCRWK is a Monte Carlo estimator of the random walk kernel whose per-pair cost does not depend on graph size, so it avoids building the product graph.
AI.motivation: Computing the random walk kernel exactly requires the product graph, and existing alternatives such as Graph Voyagers are slower on large graphs.
AI.method: It normalises the kernel coefficients, samples a shared walk length and estimates its contribution with random walks on the input graphs. For a fixed expected walk length and efficient neighbour sampling, each pairwise estimate takes O(m) time for m Monte Carlo samples, so the sample budget trades runtime against accuracy.
AI.result: On large synthetic graphs MCRWK is faster than Graph Voyagers and, at matched runtime, more accurate. It has the lowest Gram-matrix runtime on the five real datasets studied.
AI.conclusion: MCRWK gives a simple, tunable approximation of the random walk kernel that scales to large graphs.

title: RC Prediction: A Python Package for Parameter-Aware Reservoir Computing
summary: A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.

AI.tldr: rc_prediction is an open-source Python package for parameter-aware reservoir computing, which learns from time series at several parameter values and predicts trajectories at parameter values never observed.
AI.motivation: A data-driven model of a nonlinear system should capture how its dynamics change with a parameter, including qualitative changes at bifurcations, not only reproduce one operating condition.
AI.method: Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) supplies the parameter through an extra input channel and runs the trained reservoir in closed loop as an autonomous system. The package provides multi-parameter training, closed-loop prediction, parameter scans, a standard echo state network, hyperparameter optimisation and optional PyTorch GPU acceleration.
AI.result: Three benchmark dynamical systems demonstrate the workflow. In a featured application, a model trained only on pre-critical data is queried beyond its training range to predict system collapse, estimate the critical parameter and characterise transient lifetimes.
AI.conclusion: The package makes parameter-aware reservoir computing usable for forecasting dynamics at unseen parameters, including critical transitions.

title: Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
summary: Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that steering vectors can guide parameter updates during LLM post-training, improving supervised distillation by up to 12% and giving a training signal for RL with verifiable rewards.
AI.motivation: Steering vectors have mainly been used as post-hoc inference-time controls, and it was unknown whether the same residual-stream directions can also guide training.
AI.method: Two intervention regimes are studied: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training (SFT and distillation), and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. Each regime is analysed along three axes: the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training.
AI.result: In supervised settings SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to 12% when distilling from thinking-mode teachers, across three random seeds. In RL, a correctness-contrast direction used for advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including all-wrong groups, transfers to held-out math benchmarks and composes with entropy-aware advantage shaping. Three failure boundaries are identified: code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time use on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the regime.
AI.conclusion: Steering vectors are a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training.

title: When Can Unlabeled Data Pools Replace Membership Queries?
summary: Membership queries let a learner label arbitrary points and give near-optimal $\tilde O(n\log(1/\eps))$ label complexity for halfspaces under every marginal. A pool learner may label only sampled points. We ask when unlabeled data can replace membership queries. For homogeneous halfspaces the answer depends only on the angular law of $X/\|X\|$. If this law assigns zero mass to every hyperplane through the origin and positive mass to every nonempty open set of directions together with its reflection, a pool learner uses $O(n\log^3n\log(n/(\eps\delta)))$ labels, uniformly over all such marginals and targets, without density, moment, concavity or isotropy assumptions. The same label bound holds for non-homogeneous halfspaces under every marginal with full support and no mass on affine hyperplanes, including Gaussians. Dropping either angular assumption admits $\Omega(1/\eps)$ pool versus $O(\log(1/\eps))$ membership-query separations, even with unlimited unlabeled data. The price is paid in unlabeled data: in dimension $n\ge3$, for every unlabeled budget fixed in advance, some marginal satisfying both assumptions forces $\Omega(1/\eps)$ labels. For isotropic $s$-concave marginals in dimension $n\ge3$, unlimited pools keep logarithmic label rates for every finite $s$. With an unlabeled budget fixed in advance, class-uniform polylogarithmic rates hold exactly for $s>-1/(n+1)$, or $s>-1/n$ under central symmetry, and in the general class the optimal rate between these thresholds is $\tilde\Theta(\eps^{-(n-2)/n})$. This extends the range $s\ge-1/(2n+3)$ of previous sample-based guarantees, in the realizable setting.

AI.tldr: The paper characterises when unlabeled data pools can replace membership queries for learning halfspaces, with near-logarithmic label rates under angular conditions and sharp unlabeled-data costs for isotropic s-concave marginals.
AI.motivation: Membership queries give near-optimal label complexity for halfspaces, but a pool learner may label only sampled points, and it was unclear when unlabeled data can substitute for queries.
AI.method: For homogeneous halfspaces the answer depends on the angular law of X/||X||: zero mass on every hyperplane through the origin and positive mass on every open set of directions together with its reflection. For non-homogeneous halfspaces the analogous condition is full support with no mass on affine hyperplanes. Separation and unlabeled-budget results are derived for isotropic s-concave marginals.
AI.result: Under the angular assumptions a pool learner uses O(n log^3 n log(n/(eps delta))) labels, uniformly over marginals and targets. Dropping either angular assumption gives Omega(1/eps) pool versus O(log(1/eps)) membership-query separations, even with unlimited unlabeled data. In dimension n at least 3, a fixed unlabeled budget forces Omega(1/eps) labels for some marginal satisfying both assumptions. For isotropic s-concave marginals, class-uniform polylogarithmic rates hold exactly for s above -1/(n+1), or above -1/n under central symmetry, and the optimal rate between these thresholds is Theta-tilde(eps^(-(n-2)/n)), extending the earlier range s at least -1/(2n+3).
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled pools can replace membership queries under angular conditions, but the price is paid in unlabeled data, with sharp thresholds for s-concave marginals.

title: MOSAIC: Addressing Disproportionate Task-Modality Dependencies via Modality-Partitioned Gradient Routing
summary: In multi-task settings, combining multiple modalities allows task representations to draw on signals that a single modality alone would not capture. However, individual tasks may depend disproportionately on particular modalities, a structure that conventional fusion-based architectures do not model explicitly, instead enforcing a unified representation space. Consequently, a task's gradients can affect parameters tied to modalities it barely relies on, leaving features that compromise between competing demands. Although prior work has explored task-weighting and loss-balancing strategies, their effectiveness is limited by the absence of explicit modality separation, preventing models from optimising each modality according to its task-specific importance. To address these limitations, we propose MOSAIC (MOdality-Separated Architecture with Inter-modal Cross-attention), which preserves unimodal representations while enabling controlled interaction between them, and uses modality-specific losses to route gradients to their corresponding partitions. On the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation (CEJC), MOSAIC improves average macro-F1 by 7.4 points across four tasks with a 72% reduction in backbone parameters relative to a fusion-based baseline. Our results demonstrate that modality partitioning yields consistent gains across tasks while requiring far fewer backbone parameters than a fusion-based design.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC is a modality-partitioned architecture that keeps unimodal representations separate and routes gradients through modality-specific losses, improving average macro-F1 by 7.4 points on CEJC with 72% fewer backbone parameters.
AI.motivation: Fusion-based multi-task models enforce one unified representation, so a task's gradients reach parameters tied to modalities it barely relies on, and task-weighting or loss-balancing cannot fix this without explicit modality separation.
AI.method: MOdality-Separated Architecture with Inter-modal Cross-attention. It preserves unimodal representations while allowing controlled interaction between them, and uses modality-specific losses to route gradients to their corresponding partitions.
AI.result: On the Corpus of Everyday Japanese Conversation (CEJC), average macro-F1 improves by 7.4 points across four tasks relative to a fusion-based baseline, with a 72% reduction in backbone parameters.
AI.conclusion: Modality partitioning gives consistent gains across tasks while requiring far fewer backbone parameters than a fusion-based design.

title: Towards Understanding Score-Seeking in LLMs
summary: Production large language models sometimes reward-hack, exploiting flaws in how tasks are scored rather than performing the tasks as intended, sometimes in highly sophisticated and adversarial ways. We investigate the motivations driving this behavior in GPT 5.6 Sol, GPT 5.5, and a checkpoint of OpenAI o3 without safety training ("exp-rl-cap-late") by observing model behavior in agentic environments where the grader is leaked. In our environments, the models appear to be score-seeking: trying to score well according to graders that they believe assess their current actions, even at the expense of violating explicit user instructions.
