Evaluated on a decade of southeast Texas rainfall, it produces close counterparts for 4-5% of the most severe 2% of storms, compared with 3% for stochastic storm transposition.
AI.motivation: Historically rare storms are occurring with unprecedented frequency, while infrastructure is designed around short observational records that sparse data cannot adequately represent.
AI.method: A generative machine-learning model transforms an observed storm's initial hours into complete hourly rainfall lifecycles in minutes, with the aim of producing physically plausible scenarios.
AI.result: StormGen produced close counterparts for 4-5% of the most severe 2% of storms, compared with 3% for stochastic storm transposition, and maintained spatial coherence over full 24-hour sequences. From a single hour of initial rainfall it reconstructed the lifecycle, spatial pattern, and extreme catchment totals of Hurricane Harvey, although Harvey is entirely absent from training.
AI.conclusion: Complete generated scenarios give a way to stress-test flood protections against unprecedented extremes, since storm timing alone can more than double peak flows.

title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
summary: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.

AI.tldr: The paper compares replacement operators for training-free mixture-of-experts expert pruning with the mask held fixed, and finds that the survivors' gate scale is the largest effect. It introduces the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank replacement that adds 1.2-1.8% parameters at 50% pruning and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant replacement on OLMoE and Moonlight.
AI.motivation: Published training-free expert pruning methods change both which experts are removed and what the layer computes when the router still selects a removed expert, so the two effects are confounded.
AI.method: With the mask fixed, the paper compares replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. It introduces the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant.
AI.result: On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. The tilted novice gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates. At 25% pruning, MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling does.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation choices can change conclusions in expert pruning studies, and the paper proposes a five-item reporting checklist.

title: Anomalies as Residuals: Cauchy Displacement Networks
summary: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR remain among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but they compare every query with the stored training set, so their inference cost and memory grow with the data and the data must be kept at deployment. We ask whether the neighbourhood geometry these detectors exploit can be compiled into a small network that scores a query with a single forward pass. We propose the Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN), which regresses each normal point onto the mean of its $k$ nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. This displacement is an empirical mean-shift vector, whose fixed-radius population counterpart locally approximates a scaled gradient of the log density. We show that Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-$t$ expert densities, and establish a constructive approximation bound for the corresponding population neighbourhood-mean map using a single-hidden-layer Cauchy network. We further show that the bounded network output guarantees asymptotically linear residual-score growth along every fixed direction. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, while scoring $10^4$ queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.

AI.tldr: The Cauchy Displacement Network (CDN) compiles the neighbourhood geometry of tabular anomaly detectors into a single-hidden-layer network that scores a query in one forward pass, by regressing each normal point onto the mean of its k nearest training neighbours and scoring by the length of the predicted displacement. On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines it obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR.
AI.motivation: Neighbourhood-based detectors such as KNN, LOF and LUNAR are among the most accurate methods for tabular anomaly detection, but their inference cost and memory grow with the data, which must be kept at deployment.
AI.method: CDN regresses each normal point onto the mean of its k nearest training neighbours with a single-hidden-layer network of Cauchy activations and scores a query by the length of its predicted displacement. Cauchy units exactly represent the score fields of a structured family of Student-t expert densities.
AI.result: On 46 benchmark datasets against 28 baselines, CDN obtains the best mean rank under both AUC-ROC and AUC-PR, and it scores 10^4 queries in a few milliseconds on a single CPU thread, up to three orders of magnitude faster than neighbourhood-based detectors, with a model whose size does not depend on the training set.
AI.conclusion: Neighbourhood geometry can be compiled into a compact network that scores queries without storing the training data at deployment, with a constructive approximation bound supporting the population version.

title: Certifying Retraining Regret through Residual Structure
comment: 46 pages, 5 figures. Code and reproduction materials: this https URL
summary: We certify a fixed ridge predictor's regret against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table. Our main theorem gives verifiable original-row residual conditions for a uniform error bound independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank, with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Full-rank constructions separate certification dimension from feature dimension, including examples requiring directions beyond the candidate. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result. Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width $10^{-5}$. Their primary median widths improve over centered moments. Joint residual refinement additionally certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a concrete fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds, versus five for moments. Refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.

AI.tldr: The paper certifies the regret of a fixed ridge predictor against full-feature retraining over every continuous completion of an interval-valued table, with a uniform error bound that is independent of nuisance-feature scale and rank. Four real-world tasks certify twenty rank-three instances to a width of 10^-5.
AI.motivation: Whether a fixed predictor remains close to full-feature retraining is hard to decide when table entries are known only as intervals, and the paper addresses this with verifiable certificates.
AI.method: Verifiable original-row residual conditions give a uniform error bound with an asymptotically sharp leading constant and quantitative leakage stability. Observed-row anchors make the conditions computable, while exact row geometry and global search return valid upper bounds and feasible original-table witnesses. A finite-scale contraction and a common-domain moment fallback implement the structural result.
AI.result: Four real-world tasks retain all model features and certify twenty rank-three instances to width 10^-5, with primary median widths improving over centered moments. Joint residual refinement certifies all twenty new response-independent masks to the same precision within 76.21 seconds. For a fixed-point predictor contract, pure energy certifies thirteen of fifteen stopping decisions in ten seconds versus five for moments, and refinement certifies all fifteen within 91.68 seconds at the same objective threshold.
AI.conclusion: Residual-structure certificates are practical and tighter than the moment baseline, and joint refinement certifies all cases at the target precision.

title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
summary: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.

AI.tldr: SparseGDN is a hardware-aware framework for long-context prefill of Gated Delta Networks that combines a structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent selection of recurrent-state updates. Retaining about 29% of recurrent events on average, it achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.motivation: Gated Delta Networks offer linear-time sequence modelling, yet long-context prefill remains costly because of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage.
AI.method: A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, and a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
AI.result: Evaluated on RULER tasks at context lengths from 4K to 128K on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, retaining about 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
AI.conclusion: Selective recurrent updates and compact state handling reduce both computation and memory traffic in GDN prefill while still producing outputs for every token.

title: A Unified XAI-NSAI Analytical Framework for Trustworthy IoT Anomaly Detection
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT), 2026
summary: The widespread deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in critical environments makes anomaly detection essential for identifying abnormal behaviors and supporting timely investigation and response. However, accurate detection alone is insufficient. Practical IoT deployments must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge and reasoning, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making. Although recently proposed approaches increasingly incorporate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) or Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NSAI), XAI and NSAI methods are often considered independently. We argue that they should be considered together to better understand their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection. To address this gap, we propose a unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions. The framework provides a structured basis for characterizing existing approaches, identifying capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guiding the design of new anomaly detection systems for different IoT applications. We demonstrate the framework's analytical utility by applying it to three representative studies and illustrate its design utility through its application to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified analytical framework that treats explainable AI (XAI) and neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) together for trustworthy IoT anomaly detection, organized around five complementary dimensions. It is applied to three representative studies and to the design of a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.
AI.motivation: XAI and NSAI are often considered independently, although practical IoT anomaly detection must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making.
AI.method: A unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions, used to characterize existing approaches, identify capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guide the design of new anomaly detection systems.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. The framework's analytical utility is shown by applying it to three representative studies, and its design utility by applying it to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.
AI.conclusion: Considering XAI and NSAI together clarifies their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection.

title: From Representation to Readout: Mechanistic Analysis of Membership Signals in Language Models
summary: Membership inference aims to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. Such membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, while the underlying mechanisms can involve both how information is represented internally and how it is accessed by the model to produce behaviors. We therefore present a mechanistic study of membership signals in large language models (LLMs). We introduce Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap (DUG), a set of complementary measures that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and the extent to which it is exposed through the model's readout. Across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout under SFT, while under RL-based membership inference methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching further localizes this membership-specific effect to intermediate layers. To examine whether these findings extend to a more general RL setting, we further study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution. In this setting, we find that behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DUG, three complementary measures (Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap) that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and how much of it the model's readout exposes. Membership effects appear in both decodable information and readout under SFT, but primarily in readout under RL-based membership inference.
AI.motivation: Membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, yet their mechanisms involve both how information is represented internally and how the model accesses it to produce behavior, and these two parts have not been separated.
AI.method: The paper introduces DUG and uses it in a mechanistic study of membership signals across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods. Activation patching localizes the membership-specific effect, and the study extends to RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution.
AI.result: Under SFT, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout; under RL-based methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching localizes the effect to intermediate layers. In the RLVR contamination setting, behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.
AI.conclusion: Membership signals have representation and readout components whose relative weight depends on the training method, and behavior can change without a detectable likelihood-based membership signal.

title: Task Vectors Can Be Linearly Decomposed into Interpretable and Controllable Components
summary: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.

AI.tldr: Decomposes a task vector (TV) used to steer LLMs into task recognition (TR), task learning (TL) and residual components built from candidate-label unembeddings, and optimises the TR and TL coefficients with Bayesian optimisation; the resulting interventions outperform the original TVs.
AI.motivation: Task vectors are used to steer LLMs but are treated as atomised directions whose internal functional structure is poorly understood, although in-context learning has been decomposed into task recognition and task learning.
AI.method: A TR/TL-based decomposition separates each TV into TR, TL and residual components using candidate-label unembeddings, and the TR and TL coefficients are tuned with Bayesian optimisation for intervention; evaluated across several model families, classification tasks, and instruction- and demonstration-based TVs.
AI.result: TR/TL-based optimisation yields intervention directions that outperform the original TVs; optimising over random directions also helps, but TR/TL search gives more reliable gains, especially for instruction-based TVs; isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects consistent with their intended functional roles.
AI.conclusion: Task vectors are not monolithic steering directions and can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.

title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.

AI.tldr: Evaluates seven frontier LLMs on in-context molecular property prediction with self-reported uncertainty across four datasets, comparing them with classical baselines; on the three clean datasets the best LLM matches or beats the baselines at larger context sizes, but the self-reported uncertainty ranks errors only weakly.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used in many domains, but their use for molecular property prediction is little explored, and it is unknown whether they can indicate reliably when they are wrong.
AI.method: Seven frontier LLMs predict molecular properties from in-context examples (up to 30) together with a self-reported uncertainty, and are compared against classical baselines trained on the same molecules; the four datasets are screened for training-data contamination, with ESOL, which most models have memorised, used as a comparison.
AI.result: On the clean datasets every LLM improves with more context, and at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline; the requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little; self-reported uncertainty has Spearman rank correlations with prediction errors of up to 0.46, about the level of the baseline uncertainties; on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes, while on BACE and antiviral the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline; on the contaminated ESOL dataset there is no improvement with context size.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can be competitive in-context molecular property predictors, but their self-reported uncertainty is only weakly informative, and on memorised data they gain nothing from context and report smaller uncertainty for molecules they recall, so contamination must be screened for.

title: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
summary: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exchange states between language models. How a VLM can pass visual information to a separately pretrained text-only SLM though remains unexplored. We propose \textbf{Latent-Lens}, a lightweight codec that bridges the representation gap between a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM directly in latent space, enabling them to communicate purely through hidden states. The codec consists of a domain encoder that projects hidden states from the VLM into the SLM's embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA that teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes, while training only ${\sim}1.6$M parameters (0.2\% of the combined model size). On visual question answering (CLEVR, GQA), Latent-Lens achieves $81.0\pm7.9$\% and $65.4\pm5.4$\%, compared with $58.3\pm5.7$\% and $61.8\pm1.0$\% for text communication with the same LoRA budget (+30.2--69.8pp relative to frozen text communication), while on image captioning (Flickr8k) it improves over the same baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 frozen). We also evaluate Latent-Lens with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which use different architectures, vocabularies, and hidden dimensions.

AI.tldr: Latent-Lens is a lightweight codec that passes hidden states from a frozen VLM to a frozen small language model (SLM) through a domain encoder and a LoRA attention decoder, training about 1.6M parameters, and improves visual question answering and captioning over text communication with the same LoRA budget.
AI.motivation: Modular VLM-SLM systems exchange information as discrete text, a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained visual detail that hurts small language models most; latent communication has been explored between language models, but not from a VLM to a separately pretrained text-only SLM.
AI.method: A domain encoder projects VLM hidden states into the SLM embedding space, and an attention decoder formalised as a LoRA teaches the SLM to attend to these visual prefixes; about 1.6M parameters are trained (0.2% of the combined model) while both models stay frozen.
AI.result: On CLEVR and GQA visual question answering Latent-Lens reaches 81.0±7.9% and 65.4±5.4%, against 58.3±5.7% and 61.8±1.0% for text communication with the same LoRA budget; on Flickr8k captioning it improves over that baseline by +16.5 (+18.8 against frozen text communication); it also works with TinyLlama-1.1B and InternVL2-1B, which differ in architecture, vocabulary and hidden dimension.
AI.conclusion: Passing hidden states directly in latent space is a cheap and effective alternative to text for connecting a frozen VLM and a frozen SLM, and it carries over to models with different architectures, vocabularies and hidden dimensions.

title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.

AI.tldr: Argues that the quantities reported in continual learning depend on the level they refer to (underlying data, partition into tasks, or learner), and shows with teacher-student experiments that partition granularity, presentation order and data similarity each change the measured outcome.
AI.motivation: Continual learning measurements depend on factors such as task similarity, rate of change and presentation order, but the level at which each factor is defined is usually left implicit, so reported results are ambiguous.
AI.method: Separates the three levels at which these factors can be defined and identifies which properties take a value at each; runs controlled teacher-student experiments that repartition the same trajectory at different granularities, change the presentation order and vary the similarity structure; reviews representative benchmarks for which properties they state.
AI.result: Repartitioning the same underlying trajectory at different granularities, changing the presentation order, and varying the similarity structure of the data each produce different measured outcomes; the review finds that these properties are not consistently stated by representative benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reported continual learning measurements should state the level at which their properties are defined, and where the training data is undisclosed, as in foundation models, the model's initial state inherits its data properties and the subsequent training can be described.

title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
comment: 43 pages, 10 figures, 21 tables, including Supplementary Information
summary: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. On CODE-Test, LYNX-ECG reaches a macro F1 score of 0.889, outperforming five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while its graphs need about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Because each node maps to a specific ECG time, we can delete clinically defined waveform regions and alter beat timing to audit predictions. For conduction disorders, the clinically expected region was the strongest evidence in more than 90% of correct predictions. Bradycardia and tachycardia calls follow heart rate with conduction intervals held fixed, and atrial fibrillation calls vanish when beat-to-beat variation is removed. Sparse visibility graphs thus pair accurate ECG classification with clinically grounded, testable explanations.

AI.tldr: LYNX-ECG is a graph neural network that classifies each heartbeat from a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points, reaching macro F1 0.889 on CODE-Test, above five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while staying auditable.
AI.motivation: Accurate deep-learning ECG classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions, whereas physicians read ECGs from waveform shape and timing.
AI.method: Each heartbeat is represented as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points and classified by a graph neural network; because each node maps to a specific ECG time, clinically defined waveform regions can be deleted and beat timing altered to audit the predictions.
AI.result: On CODE-Test LYNX-ECG reaches macro F1 0.889, outperforming five baselines including ECGFounder, with graphs needing about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample; for conduction disorders the clinically expected region was the strongest evidence in more than 90% of correct predictions; bradycardia and tachycardia calls follow heart rate with conduction intervals held fixed, and atrial fibrillation calls vanish when beat-to-beat variation is removed.
AI.conclusion: Sparse visibility graphs pair accurate ECG classification with clinically grounded explanations that can be tested by intervention.

title: On-device Detection of Wearer-induced NLOS on Chest-worn UWB Tags: Machine Learning, Link Indicators, or Both?
comment: Submitted to ACM Transactions on Sensor Networks
summary: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.

AI.tldr: Compares existing on-device machine-learning and UWB link-indicator classifiers for detecting wearer-induced NLOS on chest-worn tags, proposes hybrid classifiers that exploit their complementarity, and releases a recommender tool that selects a classifier under user-defined constraints.
AI.motivation: Wearer-induced NLOS causes large UWB ranging errors on worn tags and must be detected on the device under tight runtime and energy limits that ML classifiers often struggle to meet; link-indicator classifiers are faster and lighter but have rarely been explored.
AI.method: Studies existing ML and link-indicator classifiers, proposes hybrid classifiers, and analyses 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects and orientations for chest-worn tags.
AI.result: All classifiers achieve good accuracy, but relative performance, including the ranging error caused by misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration; runtime and energy vary dramatically, and some techniques give marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6 times more energy.
AI.conclusion: Classifier choice has to balance accuracy, runtime and energy, and the released recommender tool and dataset help identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints.

title: Towards Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Quantification for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials via Pre-Training
summary: Informative uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the practical deployment of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), as it provides insight into their reliability across chemical space. Although numerous post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods for MLIPs have recently been proposed, most have been trained in low-data regimes, restricting their applicability to narrow domains of interest. Inspired by the emergence of foundational MLIPs, we propose pre-training uncertainty estimators on large, diverse datasets to enable broader applicability. We pre-train several UQ models on large materials science datasets to quantify the uncertainty of different MLIPs, and evaluate their performance on both in-distribution and out-of-domain (OOD) adsorption-energy predictions. We find that pre-trained uncertainty estimators provide viable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across multiple datasets, while fine-tuning consistently yields positive correlations between predicted uncertainty and prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets. These results lay the groundwork for foundational UQ models for MLIPs, ultimately facilitating their deployment in practical settings by providing users with a priori information about model reliability and applicability.

AI.tldr: Proposes pre-training uncertainty estimators on large materials-science datasets so that they give zero-shot uncertainty for machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and shows that fine-tuned estimators give uncertainty that correlates positively with prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc uncertainty estimators for MLIPs have mostly been trained in low-data regimes, which restricts them to narrow domains, while foundational MLIPs suggest a route to broader applicability.
AI.method: Several UQ models are pre-trained on large, diverse materials-science datasets to quantify the uncertainty of different MLIPs, and are evaluated on in-distribution and out-of-domain adsorption-energy predictions.
AI.result: Pre-trained estimators give viable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across multiple datasets, while fine-tuning consistently yields positive correlations between predicted uncertainty and prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets.
AI.conclusion: The results lay the groundwork for foundational UQ models for MLIPs, giving users a priori information about model reliability and applicability in practical deployment.

title: Backpropagation-free Deep Learning for Time-Series Classification
summary: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $\rho$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.

AI.tldr: Adapts three backpropagation-free learning rules (DFA, DRTP and NoProp) to 1D convolutional networks for univariate time-series classification and studies them on 112 UCR datasets; the optimised learners reach mean F1 of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84).
AI.motivation: Time-series classification networks are trained almost exclusively by backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem, while backpropagation-free rules have been evaluated almost only on 2D image benchmarks.
AI.method: DFA, DRTP and NoProp are adapted to univariate time series with 1D convolutional architectures, with one hyperparameter-optimised configuration per method; an analysis framework relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime, tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, and measures this as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control.
AI.result: Mean F1 is 0.76 to 0.79 against ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84); intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap (partial Spearman rho from 0.28 to 0.40); pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD -0.025 and -0.055) while NoProp tolerates it (DD +0.013); relative to backpropagation, DRTP reduces training FLOPs by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA gives no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.
AI.conclusion: Backpropagation-free learners remain behind strong time-series baselines, and their computational and memory trade-offs depend on series length and architecture.

title: Exploring Bad Minima in Transfer Learning
comment: 57 pages, 13 figures, 3 tables. MPhil thesis, University of Cambridge, 2022. Supervised by Ferenc Huszár
summary: Transfer learning is a highly successful learning paradigm in deep learning which leverages knowledge from one task and applies it to another. Despite its success, the necessary conditions for knowledge transfer are unclear and require further research. In this dissertation, our aim is to understand transferability a little better by answering the following question: Does good generalization on a source task necessarily imply transferability to a related target task? We hypothesize the answer is negative, and attempt to find counterexamples via adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Over three types of adversarial attacks, our empirical results show a strong relationship between generalization on the source task and transferability. These results do not rule out generalization on the source task as a sufficient condition for successful transfer.

AI.tldr: A dissertation testing whether good generalisation on a source task guarantees transferability to a related target task, using adversarial attacks on the transfer-learning procedure; it finds a strong relationship between source-task generalisation and transferability.
AI.motivation: The conditions needed for knowledge transfer in transfer learning are unclear, and it is not known whether good source-task generalisation is sufficient for successful transfer.
AI.method: The author hypothesises that source-task generalisation is not sufficient and searches for counterexamples using three types of adversarial attacks on the transfer procedure.
AI.result: Across the three attack types there is a strong relationship between generalisation on the source task and transferability, so no counterexamples were found.
AI.conclusion: The results do not rule out source-task generalisation as a sufficient condition for successful transfer, though they do not establish it either.

title: Continual Reinforcement Learning Is an Integration Problem
comment: 39 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Playable companion and source code: this https URL
summary: This paper presents an opinionated set of ten desiderata intended to inform the design and evaluation of reinforcement-learning agents that learn continually throughout a continuing lifetime. We use these desiderata to examine a representative selection of existing approaches. Progress on individual desiderata is valuable, but the longer-term aim should be to integrate all ten within a single agent. To our knowledge, no published evaluation has yet provided evidence for such an integration. Likewise, the representative benchmarks we review probe different parts of this target, but separate evaluations do not establish that the corresponding properties coexist within one agent throughout a continuing lifetime. As a secondary contribution, we therefore present a compact persistent-world scenario as a playable companion to the desiderata and outline a proposed benchmark that examines a broad range of associated behavioral capabilities together within one such lifetime.

AI.tldr: Presents ten desiderata for reinforcement-learning agents that learn continually over a lifetime, reviews existing approaches against them, and argues that all ten should be integrated in one agent, with a persistent-world scenario and a proposed benchmark as companions.
AI.motivation: Progress on individual desiderata for continual RL is valuable, but no published evaluation shows that they coexist within one agent, and existing benchmarks probe separate parts of the target.
AI.method: An opinionated set of ten desiderata is used to examine a representative selection of existing approaches; a compact persistent-world scenario is presented as a playable companion, and a benchmark is outlined that tests the associated behaviours together within one continuing lifetime.
AI.result: No published evaluation so far provides evidence that all ten desiderata are integrated within a single agent, and separate evaluations do not establish that the corresponding properties coexist over a continuing lifetime.
AI.conclusion: The longer-term aim is to integrate all ten desiderata in a single agent, and the proposed scenario and benchmark are intended to test whether that integration holds.

title: DIFFNAS: Predictor-Free Neural Architecture Search via Diffusion Model and Zero-Cost Evaluation
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Yize Sun and Hanzhang Ma contributed equally
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has advanced the automated design of deep networks, but remains computationally expensive due to reliance on model training or performance predictors. We introduce DIFFNAS, a predictor-free NAS framework that leverages a discrete graph diffusion model guided by zero-cost performance proxies. Unlike prior diffusion-based NAS methods that require learned performance predictors, DIFFNAS conditions the generative process on training-free metrics such as MeCo and SWAP, enabling efficient architecture search with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on NAS-Bench-201 show that DIFFNAS finds the optimal architectures for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (94.37% and 73.51%) without a pretrained predictor, while reducing search cost by up to 17.5x compared to DiffusionNAG. On the MobileNetV3 search space, its accuracy is lower than that of DiffusionNAG. These results highlight the promise of diffusion models combined with zero-cost proxies for scalable and effective architecture search.

AI.tldr: DIFFNAS is a predictor-free neural architecture search method that uses a discrete graph diffusion model conditioned on zero-cost proxies (MeCo and SWAP), finding the optimal architectures on NAS-Bench-201 for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with up to 17.5 times lower search cost than DiffusionNAG.
AI.motivation: NAS is computationally expensive because it relies on model training or learned performance predictors, and prior diffusion-based NAS methods require such predictors.
AI.method: A discrete graph diffusion model generates architectures, and its generative process is conditioned on the training-free metrics MeCo and SWAP, so no performance predictor is needed.
AI.result: On NAS-Bench-201 DIFFNAS finds the optimal architectures for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (94.37% and 73.51%) without a pretrained predictor, reducing search cost by up to 17.5 times compared with DiffusionNAG; on the MobileNetV3 search space its accuracy is lower than that of DiffusionNAG.
AI.conclusion: Combining diffusion models with zero-cost proxies is a promising route to scalable and effective architecture search, although it does not beat DiffusionNAG on MobileNetV3.

title: ElTab: Elastically Looped Tabular Transformers
summary: Tabular transformer models such as TabPFN achieve strong predictive performance but incur substantial inference costs, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained settings. While looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing, they can lose significant predictive power when stopped early. To address this challenge, we introduce the Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer (ElTab), a single model trained to operate across different computational budgets through supervision at randomly sampled early exits. Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, a single ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs. These results show that elastic-depth training yields a single model that adapts to the deployment budget at hand, offering a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computational cost.

AI.tldr: ElTab trains a single elastically looped tabular transformer with supervision at randomly sampled early exits, so one model operates across computational budgets and matches several depth-specific looped models and a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline on 30 OpenML classification datasets.
AI.motivation: Tabular transformers such as TabPFN are accurate but costly at inference, and looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing but can lose much predictive power when stopped early.
AI.method: The Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer is trained with supervision at randomly sampled early exits, so a single model can run at different depths to fit the available budget.
AI.result: Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, one ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Elastic-depth training yields one model that adapts to the deployment budget and offers a favourable trade-off between predictive performance, storage and computational cost.

title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
summary: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.

AI.tldr: TVQ applies straight-through estimation to vector quantisation of LLM weights, making the quantised parameters trainable by gradient descent within a block-wise knowledge-distillation framework, and reaches near-lossless 2-bit quantisation of LLaMA2-70B with about a 1% accuracy drop on popular QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Extreme VQ compression degrades LLM performance, and recovering it is hard because VQ parameters are discrete; existing training-free methods are limited to minimising layer-wise reconstruction loss.
AI.method: Latent weights are made trainable with straight-through estimation so that gradient descent can minimise arbitrary objectives; this is applied in a block-wise knowledge-distillation paradigm, with several practical solutions to accelerate training.
AI.result: TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes and achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantisation with a modest training budget; it gives near-lossless 2-bit quantisation of LLaMA2-70B with only a 1% accuracy drop on popular QA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Gradient-based optimisation of vector-quantised LLMs is practical and effective for low-bit post-training quantisation, with a straightforward PyTorch implementation.

title: On k-nearest-neighbor regression in metric spaces
summary: We study mean squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbor regression for metric space valued features. For a fixed feature distribution mu with atomless distance distributions, we describe how neighbor selection redistributes probability through the density of a uniformly chosen neighbor of an independent query. This gives separate conditions for the approximation error and the conditional response variance, and weakens Stone's domination condition when stronger response moments are available. In particular, when k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to zero, a uniform L2(mu) bound on the selection densities suffices under a finite fourth response moment. We give a corresponding condition in terms of neighborhoods of fixed population mass and recover the Euclidean density bound. Finite global Nagata dimension gives Stone's domination. While sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality is known to ensure universal consistency of k-NN classification in complete separable spaces, we show that this is not the case for mean squared consistency with unbounded responses: we construct a space in this class on which one fixed noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error.

AI.tldr: Studies mean squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbour regression for metric-space-valued features, giving conditions that ensure it, and shows that with unbounded responses it can fail on a space in the class where universal consistency of k-NN classification holds.
AI.motivation: Consistency of k-NN regression with metric-valued features depends on how neighbour selection redistributes probability, and it was unknown whether the classification result for sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality carries over to mean squared error.
AI.method: For a fixed feature distribution with atomless distance distributions, the density of a uniformly chosen neighbour of an independent query is analysed to separate the approximation error from the conditional response variance; conditions are derived from a uniform L2 bound on selection densities, from neighbourhoods of fixed population mass, and from Nagata dimension.
AI.result: When k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to zero, a uniform L2 bound on the selection densities suffices under a finite fourth response moment; finite global Nagata dimension gives Stone's domination condition; the Euclidean density bound is recovered; and a space in the sigma-finite Nagata class is constructed on which one fixed noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error.
AI.conclusion: Sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality, which ensures universal consistency of k-NN classification, does not ensure mean squared consistency of k-NN regression with unbounded responses.

title: Binary Sparse Codes: Where are we on Energy Efficient Representations?
summary: Biological neural systems achieve impressive computational capabilities under tight metabolic constraints, relying on sparse cortical representations that minimise total neural activity. This combination of efficiency and representational power has motivated growing interest in sparse coding as a computational strategy for artificial systems. Artificial models designed to produce binary sparse codes span three broad paradigms, theoretical methods grounded in efficient coding, deep learning methods trained via backpropagation, and biologically plausible methods that learn through local Hebbian rules, each yielding codes whose quality depends not only on achieving low activation density but also on preserving the informational structure of the input. The latter property, however, lacks an agreed-upon quantitative definition, leaving the field without a principled basis for comparing methods. We propose a set of metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space, and apply this framework to compare four representative methods under matched conditions. The results reveal a consistent trade-off in which models that achieve high information preservation do so at the cost of sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code tend to sacrifice it. Competitive Sparse Codes, a biologically plausible approach, is the only architecture to occupy a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation. These findings frame the simultaneous satisfaction of both factors as an open challenge for the field and provide a reusable evaluation framework for measuring progress toward it.

AI.tldr: Proposes metrics that formalise information preservation as similarity preservation in binary sparse codes and uses them to compare four representative methods, finding a trade-off in which high information preservation comes at the cost of sparsity; only Competitive Sparse Codes keeps near-maximal sparsity with meaningful preservation.
AI.motivation: Binary sparse codes should be both sparse and informative, but information preservation lacks an agreed quantitative definition, so methods from efficient coding, backpropagation and Hebbian learning cannot be compared on a principled basis.
AI.method: Information preservation is formalised as similarity preservation, measuring how faithfully a binary sparse code reproduces the relational geometry of the input space; the metrics are applied to four representative methods under matched conditions.
AI.result: A consistent trade-off appears: models with high information preservation sacrifice sparsity, while models approaching the uniformity of an optimal random sparse code sacrifice information preservation; Competitive Sparse Codes is the only architecture that occupies a region of near-maximal sparsity while retaining meaningful information preservation.
AI.conclusion: Satisfying high information preservation and high sparsity at the same time remains an open challenge, and the framework provides a reusable evaluation for measuring progress toward it.

title: Observable-Specific Validity Tests for Scientific AI: Controlled Approximations and Intervention Response
summary: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a given bound. We formulate observable-specific validity records for scientific artificial intelligence (AI) that link a reduction to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and transformations or interventions. Explicit displacement and velocity certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator recover distinct convergence orders and provide sufficient validity guarantees. Exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the different coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria. Across 16 repeated neural fits, imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%. Paired transformations verify the protected scaling relation, while a coupling crossover identifies the additional information needed for response transfer. A causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association. For two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order $x^k$, we derive an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as $x^{-2k}$ and verify its full success curve numerically. Together with a 256-task evaluation interface, these results provide independently checkable tests of controlled approximation, physical transfer, and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.

AI.tldr: Introduces observable-specific validity records for scientific AI that tie a reduced model to its reference model, error measure, tolerance and interventions, with explicit certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator and exact relations for a Hubbard dimer; imposing dimensional homogeneity sharply reduces energy-scale transfer error in neural fits.
AI.motivation: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a bound, so validity has to be checked per observable, including under transformations and interventions.
AI.method: Explicit displacement and velocity certificates are derived for a singularly perturbed oscillator, exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria, 16 repeated neural fits are compared with and without dimensional homogeneity, paired transformations test the protected scaling relation, and a 256-task evaluation interface is provided.
AI.result: Imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy-scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%; for two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order x^k, an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as x^(-2k) is derived and verified numerically; a causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association.
AI.conclusion: The validity tests provide independently checkable criteria for controlled approximation, physical transfer and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.

title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
comment: 41 pages, 9 figures. Extended version of the Chronos-2 technical report (arXiv:2510.15821), adding scientific case studies (epidemiology, macroeconomics, carbon flux, hydrology, hierarchical forecasting), additional baselines, ablation studies, and calibration analysis. Code: this https URL
summary: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.

AI.tldr: Chronos-2 is a pretrained foundation model for zero-shot probabilistic forecasting that models interactions among multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, reaching state-of-the-art average accuracy on benchmarks and matching or surpassing specialised methods in several scientific settings.
AI.motivation: Most forecasting models are still trained separately for each domain-specific dataset, and existing time-series foundation models forecast each series independently, so they cannot model interactions among series or external drivers that are common in scientific applications.
AI.method: A single pretrained model infers relationships among time series directly from the historical context, handles heterogeneous covariates, and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment.
AI.result: Chronos-2 improves skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and raises win rates by 10 percentage points; it forecasts 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50 times and 1000 times faster end to end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters respectively; it matches or surpasses specialised methods in infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modelling, carbon-flux prediction and runoff simulation.
AI.conclusion: A single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems, giving zero-shot forecasts that are accurate, efficient and competitive with domain-specific methods.

title: Robust Learning of Multi-Index Models under Logconcave Distributions via Weak Partial Learners
comment: Full version of the paper appearing in FOCS 2026. The abstract was shortened due to requirements from arXiv
summary: We develop a new algorithmic framework for learning Boolean concept classes under logconcave distributions. Our framework applies to broad families of multi-index models and yields significantly faster robust learners than were previously known in these settings. It extends to partial classification and testable learning. Consequently, we obtain improved learners for several fundamental concept classes, including functions of halfspaces and multiclass linear classifiers, under logconcave marginals. Our starting point is a new boosting framework based on weak partial learners. Classical boosting approaches require often-intractable distribution-free weak learners or yield weak approximation guarantees. We show instead that weak learners for partial classification, where labels may be undefined on part of the domain, suffice for strong agnostic learning. The key challenge is that boosting requires a weak learner that succeeds under conditioned distributions that are not guaranteed to be logconcave. To address this, we develop a recursive moment-based partitioning procedure: given a logconcave distribution $X$ and a conditional version $X'$, we partition the space into polynomially many convex regions so that, on most regions, the low-degree moments of $X$ and $X'$ approximately agree. On each good region, a well-behaved multi-index model correlates with a low-degree polynomial, giving a weak hypothesis. Combining these hypotheses yields the required weak learner. A key ingredient of our approach is an efficient method for detecting moment discrepancy. Specifically, we show how to find a low-dimensional subspace that captures any non-trivial discrepancy between $X$ and $X'$, if one exists. Our approach combines spectral analysis of moment tensors with recent progress on isoperimetry for logconcave measures. This discrepancy-finding procedure may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Gives a new boosting framework based on weak partial learners that yields significantly faster robust learners for broad families of multi-index models and functions of halfspaces under logconcave distributions, with extensions to partial classification and testable learning.
AI.motivation: Classical boosting needs distribution-free weak learners, which are often intractable, or yields only weak approximation guarantees, so robust learning of these concept classes under logconcave marginals has been slow.
AI.method: Weak learners need only succeed for partial classification; a recursive moment-based partitioning splits the space into convex regions on which the low-degree moments of the logconcave distribution and its conditional version approximately agree; a spectral analysis of moment tensors, combined with recent isoperimetry results for logconcave measures, finds a low-dimensional subspace that captures any moment discrepancy.
AI.result: The framework gives significantly faster robust learners than previously known for broad families of multi-index models, and improved learners for functions of halfspaces and multiclass linear classifiers under logconcave marginals.
AI.conclusion: Weak partial learners suffice for strong agnostic learning, and the discrepancy-finding procedure may be of independent interest.

title: New Lower Bounds for Private PAC Learning
summary: We study realizable PAC learning under approximate differential privacy, and give a framework for proving lower bounds on its sample complexity. We construct classes with identical VC and Littlestone dimensions but different private sample complexities at common privacy and accuracy parameters, showing that these dimensions do not determine the sample complexity, even for improper learners. To address this we introduce the Independent Class Packing (ICP) parameter, the largest total sample complexity of classes in $\mathcal{G}$ that can be packed independently into a class $\mathcal{H}$, and prove that every $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, $(\alpha, \beta)$-PAC learner for $\mathcal{H}$, possibly improper, uses $\Omega\left(\mathrm{ICP}(\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G})/(\alpha\varepsilon)\right)$ examples. Using this framework we prove tight lower bounds for axis-aligned rectangles, union of intervals and linear subspaces and improved lower bounds for halfspaces and convex polygons. Finally we also show that for product classes, and more generally when the same classes pack into $\mathcal{H}$ and cover its domain so that target labels can be used directly, ICP characterizes private PAC sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: Proves new lower bounds on the sample complexity of realisable PAC learning under approximate differential privacy, introducing the Independent Class Packing (ICP) parameter, which characterises private sample complexity for product classes up to logarithmic factors where VC and Littlestone dimensions do not.
AI.motivation: Classes with identical VC and Littlestone dimensions can have different private sample complexities at common privacy and accuracy parameters, so these dimensions do not determine private sample complexity, even for improper learners.
AI.method: ICP(H,G) is defined as the largest total sample complexity of classes in G that can be packed independently into H, and every (epsilon,delta)-DP, (alpha,beta)-PAC learner for H is shown to use Omega(ICP(H,G)/(alpha epsilon)) examples; the bound is applied to specific classes.
AI.result: Tight lower bounds are proved for axis-aligned rectangles, unions of intervals and linear subspaces, and improved lower bounds for halfspaces and convex polygons; for product classes, and more generally when the same classes pack into H and cover its domain so that target labels can be used directly, ICP characterises private PAC sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: ICP is a general framework for lower bounds on private PAC sample complexity that goes beyond VC and Littlestone dimensions.

title: Less Loss, Fixed Weights: Logit Corrections for Forgetting
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: When a language model is fine-tuned to follow instructions, or further pretrained on a new subject, it often gets worse at predicting standard web text. This is known as "forgetting." We ask whether this loss can be undone by simple, fixed adjustments to the model's final token predictions. Across 14 pairs of base and derived models, from 1B to 7B parameters, we fitted a fixed bonus or penalty for each token (a vocabulary bias), alone or together with a temperature. On text held out from correction fitting, the largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%, with loss conditional on the retained vocabulary. Combining the bias with a temperature recovers up to 36%. Models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing. Finally, in a controlled simulation where a model is damaged at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, the bias-plus-temperature fix still recovers 29%. Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of our restricted fits.

AI.tldr: Shows that the loss language models suffer on standard web text after instruction tuning or domain pretraining can only be partly undone by fixed per-token vocabulary biases and a temperature, recovering at most 36% of the loss increase on real models.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuned or further pretrained language models often get worse at predicting standard web text, and it is unclear whether simple fixed adjustments to the final token predictions can undo this forgetting.
AI.method: Across 14 base and derived model pairs from 1B to 7B parameters, a fixed bias per token is fitted alone or together with a temperature and evaluated on text held out from the correction fitting; a controlled simulation that damages a model at random, with no planted bias or temperature change, serves as a check.
AI.result: The largest top-4K bias recovery estimate is under 10%; bias combined with temperature recovers up to 36%; models further pretrained on math lose the most and recover almost nothing; in the random-damage simulation the same fix still recovers 29%.
AI.conclusion: Most of the real-model loss increase stays out of reach of these restricted fits, so such fixed logit corrections cannot be relied on to undo forgetting, and their recovery figures must be read against the 29% obtained on random damage.

title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, where their errors compound. Jacobian-based regularisers aim to curb this growth, but in a chaotic system part of the growth is physical and cannot be trained away. We separate the two sources of this error with a first-order decomposition. We compare the emulator's error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver's Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio: the factor by which the model's own dynamics amplify its errors. We study 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes (8-10k and 33k parameters), with errors measured at one Lyapunov time. Jacobian fine-tuning reduced the error by more than 10% for 1 of 34 seeds whose amplification ratio was at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds whose ratio was at least four; for the latter, the error fell by a factor of 8 (small models) and 55 (33k models) in geometric mean over seeds. The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio. Matching the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction (EDJM) outperformed random directions at the same cost on 28 of 35 seeds; input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.

AI.tldr: Shows that Jacobian fine-tuning of neural PDE emulators helps mainly when the model's own dynamics amplify its errors, as measured by an amplification ratio from a first-order error decomposition. The gain depends on that ratio rather than on the regulariser alone.
AI.motivation: Neural emulators of chaotic PDEs are trained on one-step prediction but deployed autoregressively, so errors compound, and Jacobian regularisers cannot remove the part of the growth that is physical in a chaotic system.
AI.method: A first-order decomposition compares the emulator error with a counterfactual that propagates the same one-step mistakes through the solver Jacobian, giving an amplification ratio; 21 configurations across four PDEs, five architectures and two model sizes are studied, and Jacobian matching along the model's own error direction (EDJM) is compared with random directions and input-noise injection.
AI.result: Fine-tuning reduced error by more than 10% for only 1 of 34 seeds with amplification ratio at most 1.25, and for all 20 seeds with ratio at least four, where the geometric-mean error fell by a factor of 8 for small models and 55 for 33k-parameter models; EDJM outperformed random directions on 28 of 35 seeds, and input-noise injection performed comparably to EDJM.
AI.conclusion: The gain approximately equals the one-step accuracy cost of fine-tuning divided by the amplification ratio, so Jacobian fine-tuning is worthwhile mainly when the model's own dynamics amplify its errors.

title: Know When the Equation Is Wrong: Structural Uncertainty for LLM-Guided Symbolic Regression under Extrapolation
