summary: Large language models (LLMs) can help discover mathematical equations from data, but most LLM-guided symbolic regression methods focus on a single best equation without quantifying uncertainty over alternative functional forms. This is challenging because distinct equations can fit the observed data similarly while producing substantially different extrapolations. Our experiments on the LLM-SRBench dataset show that standard conformal intervals achieve nominal in-distribution coverage but frequently fail under extrapolation. To tackle this challenge, we introduce LLM-SR-UQ, a framework that retains competing equation structures and uses their disagreement to characterize uncertainty about the underlying functional form. We extend the standard fixed-width conformal approach to quantify structural intervals, which measure disagreement among candidate equations and identify where prediction intervals should widen. Extensive experiments show our framework substantially improves coverage attainment by incorporating structural disagreement while preserving in-distribution coverage. Our approach also shows good generalizability when it is applied to other symbolic-regression methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes LLM-SR-UQ, which keeps competing equations from LLM-guided symbolic regression and uses their disagreement to widen prediction intervals under extrapolation. It addresses the coverage failures of standard conformal intervals out of distribution.
AI.motivation: LLM-guided symbolic regression usually returns a single best equation without uncertainty over alternative functional forms, and standard conformal intervals reach nominal coverage in distribution but often fail under extrapolation.
AI.method: LLM-SR-UQ retains competing equation structures and extends fixed-width conformal prediction to structural intervals that measure disagreement among candidate equations and indicate where prediction intervals should widen; it is evaluated on LLM-SRBench and applied to other symbolic-regression methods.
AI.result: The framework substantially improves coverage attainment under extrapolation while preserving in-distribution coverage, and it generalises to other symbolic-regression methods; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement among candidate equations is a useful signal of uncertainty about the functional form, so symbolic regression should account for structural uncertainty when it extrapolates.

title: GhostPrefix: Synchronization-Free Universal Prefix Attacks for ASR Manipulation
summary: We present GhostPrefix, the first synchronization-free universal adversarial prefix attack against automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Unlike prior audio attacks, which are typically crafted per utterance, require synchronization with the victim waveform, or target narrow objectives, GhostPrefix learns a short, reusable audio segment prepended to arbitrary live speech to exert real-time control over ASR outputs without knowledge of the future utterance or temporal alignment. A key challenge is maintaining stable adversarial effects across unknown, evolving speech contexts. GhostPrefix combines token-level losses with a novel representation-level objective for stable, input-agnostic effects. GhostPrefix supports three attack modes: (i) prompted prefix attacks for semantic steering, (ii) targeted prefix attacks for transcript hijacking, and (iii) untargeted prefix attacks for transcription degradation. To remain perceptually inconspicuous, we regularize prefixes toward benign environmental-sound distributions and improve robustness against over-the-air distortions. We evaluate GhostPrefix across 13 open-source ASR models from four families. In digital settings, it achieves average attack success rates of 97.6% for prompted steering and 93.4% for targeted hijacking, while driving word error rate to 1.18 under untargeted attacks. Over the air, it achieves success rates of 91.5% and 89.5% for prompted and targeted modes, respectively. These manipulations propagate into downstream AI-assisted pipelines, including voice assistants and AI note-taking tools, causing systematic semantic misinterpretations. GhostPrefix exposes synchronization-free universal prefixes as a practical, under-explored threat to real-world ASR and downstream applications. Artifacts and demos are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces GhostPrefix, a universal adversarial audio prefix that controls ASR output in real time without knowing the upcoming speech or aligning with it. It reports high attack success rates across 13 ASR models in digital and over-the-air settings.
AI.motivation: Prior audio attacks are typically crafted per utterance, require synchronisation with the victim waveform, or target narrow objectives, which limits their use against live speech.
AI.method: A short reusable audio segment is learned by combining token-level losses with a representation-level objective for stable, input-agnostic effects; it supports prompted, targeted and untargeted modes, and its prefixes are regularised toward benign environmental-sound distributions to stay inconspicuous and robust over the air.
AI.result: Across 13 open-source ASR models from four families, digital attack success averages 97.6% for prompted steering and 93.4% for targeted hijacking, and word error rate reaches 1.18 under untargeted attacks; over the air, success is 91.5% for prompted and 89.5% for targeted modes.
AI.conclusion: Synchronisation-free universal prefixes are a practical and under-explored threat to ASR systems and to downstream pipelines such as voice assistants and AI note-taking tools.

title: CausalXRL: Explainable Reinforcement Learning through Causal Graph Reasoning
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 - full paper - main track
summary: Reinforcement learning is a powerful paradigm for training autonomous agents and has achieved impressive performance in complex environments. However, this success often comes at the cost of interpretability, diminishing trust and complicating efforts to debug and improve agent behavior. To address these challenges, we introduce CausalXRL, a novel framework for explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). A key feature of CausalXRL is its use of causal graph reasoning, which provides transparent, structured, multi-level explanations of agent decision-making. We validate CausalXRL through comprehensive case studies and a two-part evaluation: (1) a quantitative analysis of explanation fidelity and causal-structure learning efficiency in benchmark RL environments, and (2) a qualitative expert study assessing explainability in the real-time strategy (RTS) benchmark MicroRTS. The quantitative results show that CausalXRL can provide faithful explanations while efficiently learning causal structures, and the qualitative expert study suggests that participants found CausalXRL useful for inspecting high-level RTS strategies.

AI.tldr: Presents CausalXRL, an explainable reinforcement learning framework that uses causal graph reasoning to give structured, multi-level explanations of agent decisions. It is evaluated on benchmark RL environments and with an expert study on MicroRTS.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning performs strongly in complex environments, but its lack of interpretability reduces trust and makes debugging and improving agent behaviour harder.
AI.method: CausalXRL builds its explanations from causal graph reasoning, which yields transparent, structured, multi-level accounts of decision-making, and is validated through case studies and a two-part evaluation of explanation fidelity and expert assessment.
AI.result: Quantitatively, the framework gives faithful explanations while learning causal structure efficiently on benchmark RL environments; qualitatively, participants in an expert study on the MicroRTS real-time strategy benchmark found it useful for inspecting high-level strategies.
AI.conclusion: Causal graph reasoning can make RL agent decisions inspectable at several levels of abstraction, though the abstract reports no numerical results from the expert study.

title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?
summary: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.

AI.tldr: Finds that looping a trained model pays for its extra inference compute only at the smallest size tested, 0.8B, which beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B the looped model does not beat the same model trained without the loop.
AI.motivation: Adding a loop to a trained model leaves parameters, memory and training cost unchanged but makes every generated token more expensive, and it is unclear whether loops added after pretraining justify that cost.
AI.method: Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive; a looped model is compared with the same model trained identically without the loop at equal parameters, and with the best unlooped use of the same inference FLOPs, across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters.
AI.result: Only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines; at 4B and 9B the looped model does not beat the equal-parameter baseline, and the benchmarks are not too easy to separate them, since the unlooped 9B model scores up to 13 points above the 4B model.
AI.conclusion: Introducing loops into an already pretrained model pays off only for small models under a fixed parameter budget.

title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo
comment: 35 pages, 16 figures, 7 tables; supplementary tables and figures included
summary: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.

AI.tldr: Proposes an Acoustic Biodiversity Index built from species-level detections, ABI_E, a Shannon diversity normalised by the regional species pool, which tracks richness far better than six standard acoustic indices. It is tested in a Zimbabwean savanna and at an Abu Dhabi zoo.
AI.motivation: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid biodiversity proxies, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly.
AI.method: Four classifiers were benchmarked on a labelled tropical dataset, with BirdNET embeddings and logistic regression performing best; BirdNET v2.4 with location and season filters was applied to a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley and three zoo habitats, with a stricter post-hoc location filter, diel-matched rarefaction to 6 h, and a temporal stability term T reported separately.
AI.result: The savanna held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3 to 13 species (ABI_E = 0.03 to 0.21) at the zoo sites; across 149 recorded hours ABI_E correlated with richness at Spearman rho = 0.93, whereas the best standard index, ACI, reached 0.48; random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70.
AI.conclusion: Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation are a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.

title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data from Sliced Chebyshev Moments
summary: Research on practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data has largely focused on methods that approximately preserve low-dimensional marginals of a target distribution, and can thus only hope to preserve higher-dimensional, global structure as a lucky by-product. At the same time, existing methods that target global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension, $d$. In this work, we address this ``curse of dimensionality'' by presenting a new DP synthetic data algorithm, SPLICE, that comes with a compelling global distributional guarantee, even in high-dimensions, and moreover, is practically state-of-the-art. Our algorithm is based on measuring noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fitting a distribution to match, a twist on recent polynomial methods for 1-D synthetic data. We prove that, given a dataset of $n$ examples, SPLICE returns a private distribution with Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ from the target, for constant privacy parameters. Notably, this bound is independent of the data dimension, $d$. Along the way, we prove a moment matching result of independent interest: for a distribution on the unit ball, matching the first $O(1/\alpha)$ Chebyshev moments along $\tilde{O}(d/\alpha^2)$ random directions guarantees $\alpha$ Sliced Wasserstein error. Finally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior DP synthetic data methods on an extensive benchmark.

AI.tldr: Presents SPLICE, a differentially private synthetic data algorithm whose Sliced Wasserstein-1 error bound does not depend on data dimension. It fits a distribution to noisy sliced Chebyshev moments and reports state-of-the-art performance on an extensive benchmark.
AI.motivation: Practical DP synthetic data methods mostly preserve low-dimensional marginals, while methods with global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension.
AI.method: SPLICE measures noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fits a distribution to match them, a twist on polynomial methods for one-dimensional synthetic data, with a practical implementation that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature.
AI.result: For n examples and constant privacy parameters the returned distribution is within Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance of order 1/sqrt(n), up to logarithmic factors, of the target, a bound independent of dimension d; the method achieves state-of-the-art performance against prior DP synthetic data methods.
AI.conclusion: The work gives a dimension-free global distributional guarantee for DP synthetic data, together with a moment-matching result of independent interest for distributions on the unit ball.

title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
summary: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.

AI.tldr: Shows that expected-improvement (EI) stopping in freeze-thaw Bayesian optimisation can stop too early, gives a certificate that proves such stops premature, and finds EI stopping to be a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.
AI.motivation: Freeze-thaw BO usually stops at a budget or convergence test, whereas a budget-free utility of best observed score minus cost per increment needs a principled stopping rule.
AI.method: A one-step lookahead advances the candidate with the largest expected improvement under a fixed surrogate and stops once no EI exceeds the cost; the authors construct a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead as a certificate and show that repeating the correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate.
AI.result: Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs; on three hyperparameter optimisation benchmarks a pre-registered test found EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gained at low costs on two of the three.
AI.conclusion: EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference that trades lower scores for fewer training increments, and its utility rises with more information sharing in the surrogate.

title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments
comment: 9 pages main paper, 15 pages references and appendix, 17 figures. Presented at the Nineteenth European Workshop on Reinforcement Learning (EWRL 2026)
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.

AI.tldr: Studies how plasticity loss interacts with stochasticity in deep RL by training SAC agents on DeepMind Control tasks with controlled observation and action noise. Plasticity-preserving methods help on the harder tasks, and TD instability dominates in the most stochastic settings.
AI.motivation: Plasticity loss has been proposed as a cause of the brittleness of deep RL, but it has been little studied in stochastic environments.
AI.method: SAC agents are trained on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise, comparing plasticity-preserving methods, resets, and resets combined with layer normalisation.
AI.result: Plasticity-preserving methods increase robustness on the two harder tasks, with the advantage growing as observation noise rises; resets combined with layer normalisation underperform resets alone at every observation noise level tested; noise accelerates plasticity loss in harder environments but acts as a regulariser in easier ones; plasticity loss is most pronounced early in training.
AI.conclusion: In the most challenging stochastic settings TD instability, rather than gradual plasticity loss, becomes the dominant failure mode.

title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.

AI.tldr: Introduces Hyperbolic IRL, which models reward as a function of hyperbolic distance between a feature vector and a learned parameter vector, and shows it matches state-of-the-art baselines while revealing conjunctive reward structure in museum navigation.
AI.motivation: Prior IRL reward functions use linear weights, neural networks or other approximators without assumptions about the geometry of the feature space, although geometric organisation is observed in neural circuits.
AI.method: The reward is parameterised by hyperbolic distance, with a Euclidean distance variant, between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, and is tested against linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies.
AI.result: The hyperbolic approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excels in the low-data limit and across dense environments; applied to human navigation among museum exhibits, it reveals reward structure that depends on non-separable conjunctions of exhibit-distance features.
AI.conclusion: A hyperbolic reward parameterisation can improve both the predictive accuracy and the interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how conjunctive structure can explain behaviour.

title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT
summary: In the random allocation sampling scheme each user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence of $t$ steps. This scheme is known to improve on Poisson sampling in private optimization and in communication-efficient aggregation. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for this scheme runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter $\alpha$ (Feldman and Shenfeld, 2026). We give an algorithm, \emph{multiscale FFT}, that represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum using FFTs within each interval. It keeps the guarantees of the accountant and improves the dependence of its running time on $\alpha$ from $O(\alpha^{-2})$ to $O(\alpha^{-1}\log(1/\alpha))$. In addition, we demonstrate that rounding can be performed via the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of (Doroshenko et al., 2026). This reduces the errors that rounding introduces in the mean of the privacy loss and in the $\chi^2$ divergence of the computed pair from the order of $\alpha$ to $O(\alpha^2/\log(t))$. In our experiments, our algorithm achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.

AI.tldr: Introduces multiscale FFT, a privacy loss accountant for random allocation that reduces the running time's dependence on the accuracy parameter from quadratic to near-linear and tightens rounding errors. It gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.
AI.motivation: The existing PLD accountant for random allocation runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter, which limits how accurately privacy can be accounted for.
AI.method: The algorithm represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum with FFTs within each interval; rounding is performed with the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of Doroshenko et al. (2026).
AI.result: Running time improves from O(alpha^-2) to O(alpha^-1 log(1/alpha)) while keeping the accountant's guarantees, and rounding errors in the mean of the privacy loss and in the chi-squared divergence drop from order alpha to O(alpha^2/log t); experiments show speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The method makes high-accuracy PLD accounting for random allocation practical and yields improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.

title: Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics
summary: Understanding how gradient descent learns features remains a central challenge in neural network theory. We study this question in a minimal multi-index setting that already exhibits rich multi-phase gradient dynamics: a well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model under isotropic Gaussian inputs, trained by population gradient flow from small initialization. We show that the dynamics are organized by two directions: the "easy" bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and the "hard" splitting direction, which governs specialization. To characterize the loss structure and learning behavior, we analyze the population squared-loss landscape and show that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle. We then track the gradient-flow trajectory, showing that student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle before escaping and specializing to teacher neurons. Our results provide both a landscape and dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behavior that arises in a simple multi-index model and under standard algorithmic and architectural choices.

AI.tldr: Analyses gradient descent on a two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model and shows that every critical point with both student weights nonzero is either a global minimum or a saddle, with trajectories first collapsing to a bisector saddle before specialising.
AI.motivation: Understanding how gradient descent learns features is central to neural network theory, and a minimal setting that already exhibits multi-phase dynamics is needed to study it.
AI.method: A well-specified two-neuron ReLU teacher-student model with isotropic Gaussian inputs is trained by population gradient flow from small initialisation, and both the population squared-loss landscape and the gradient-flow trajectory are analysed.
AI.result: The dynamics are organised by an easy bisector direction, which carries the leading signal, and a hard splitting direction, which governs specialisation; student neurons first collapse toward a bisector saddle, then escape and specialise to the teacher neurons.
AI.conclusion: The results give both a landscape and a dynamics account of the multi-phase symmetry-breaking behaviour that arises in a simple multi-index model under standard algorithmic and architectural choices.

title: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material available as an ancillary file
summary: Objective: To distinguish the transferable predictive value of physiological trajectories from that of observation patterns in ICU mortality prediction, and to assess whether measurement timing affects performance independently of observation quantity. Materials and Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted at 48 hours using MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations progressively integrated latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3). Models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV patients and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals. The effect of measurement timing was assessed while holding the number of retained observations constant. Results: Physiological trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704). Observation-pattern features improved locally developed eICU models (R3-R2 -0.00257, 95% CI -0.00370 to -0.00146), but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision (-0.00012, 95% CI -0.00206 to +0.00208). R3 was favoured in 10 of 30 source bootstrap refits. At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the window reduced log loss relative to random retention by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2. Removing the final 12 hours increased log loss relative to count-matched random removal by 0.01947 for R3 versus 0.00822 for R2. Under reduced availability, the local R3 increment changed from beneficial to harmful. Discussion: Physiological trajectories transferred more consistently, while observation-pattern features were particularly sensitive to the timing and availability of measurements. Conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated not only in new patient populations but also under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs.

AI.tldr: Shows that physiological trajectories transfer more consistently than observation-pattern features in ICU mortality prediction, and that measurement timing affects performance independently of how many observations are retained. Models are evaluated across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV and eICU.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how much of the transferable predictive value of ICU models comes from physiological trajectories versus observation patterns, and whether measurement timing affects performance beyond the number of observations.
AI.method: In-hospital mortality is predicted at 48 hours with nested representations: latest-value snapshots (R1), longitudinal physiological summaries (R2), and measurement frequency and timing features (R3); models fitted on 7,762 MetaVision patients are tested on 21,682 MIMIC-IV and 43,878 eICU patients across 204 hospitals.
AI.result: Trajectories improved external prediction in eICU (R2 minus R1 log-loss difference -0.00922, 95% CI -0.01148 to -0.00704); observation-pattern features helped locally developed eICU models but not clearly after transfer from MetaVision; at matched observation counts, spread-out retention reduced log loss by 0.03280 for R3 versus 0.00703 for R2; under reduced availability the local R3 increment became harmful.
AI.conclusion: Clinical prediction models should be evaluated under the measurement conditions that supply their inputs, not only in new patient populations.

title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
summary: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.

AI.tldr: Presents an exact information-ledger chain that proves instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and MDPs, and locates where standard algorithms fall short of the classical limits. The chain is an identity only at its first step, and every other gap is a named defect.
AI.motivation: Instance-dependent limits for these sequential problems are proved by separate arguments, so a single accounting of where the gaps between algorithms and classical limits come from is missing.
AI.method: One chain runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimisation over alternatives and allocations; a one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances.
AI.result: Data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at per-arm counts and reward sums; classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects, most of which can be computed from an algorithm's own runs; on seven published sources the ledger locates the difference, and for identification among trained models and Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification.
AI.conclusion: The ledger gives an exact accounting of the gap between standard algorithms and classical limits, and shows that the uniform quantification is often the dominant term.

title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
summary: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).

AI.tldr: Proposes adding a random number of dummy points to privatise the batch size, which keeps DP-SGD privacy guarantees valid under batch-size leakage and truncation. The analysis covers both Poisson sampling and random allocation.
AI.motivation: Privacy amplification for Poisson sampling and random allocation requires batch sizes to stay hidden, yet observable batch sizes and truncation to a maximum batch size both increase privacy loss.
AI.method: A random number of dummy points privatises the batch size, and the analysis treats the count release as amplified by subsampling, so the expected number of dummies is asymptotically smaller than with direct non-negative noise; the mechanism is designed for efficient, relatively tight accounting and is easy to implement in a distributed setting.
AI.result: For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, the mechanism achieves better privacy-efficiency tradeoffs than the direct truncation accounting given by Ganesh (2025).
AI.conclusion: Dummy points give a practical way to keep privacy amplification valid under observable batch counts and truncation in both centralised and distributed DP-SGD.

title: A small HER2 reader for routine H&E slides: real-world deployment
comment: 32 pages, 12 figures, 17 tables (including supplementary material). Research use only. Weights and data: this https URL
summary: HER2 status decides who receives HER2-targeted therapy. Pathologists score HER2 protein by immunohistochemistry (IHC); equivocal IHC 2+ tumours, their hardest calls, wait for in situ hybridisation (ISH). We built a HER2 reader for routine H&E slides, owned end to end, as a baseline for pathologists. A 22M-parameter ViT-S/16 tile encoder was trained on public TCGA slides by self-supervision, distillation from H-optimus-0 and two rounds of JEPA refinement; five cross-validated attention-based slide classifiers average their probabilities; and an operating point is fixed on training data. Compared under one paired ten-seed protocol, readers on our encoder rank first of 7 on external validation from TCGA-BRCA to Yale-HER2 (AUC 0.812), level with readers on encoders 4 and 50 times larger. We also rebuilt PathBench's encoder benchmark on public cohorts; our replica reproduces its published order of reference encoders, and under it our encoder ranks first of 7 on TCGA-BRCA (0.689) and sits level with H-optimus-0 and Phikon on Yale-HER2 (0.897). On three external hospitals our deployed reader reaches AUC 0.82 on Yale-HER2 (about 0.81 with training slides balanced for tissue size), 0.75 on HEROHE and 0.63 on BCNB biopsies, and among HEROHE's 85 IHC 2+ cases it ranks ISH-amplified above non-amplified tumours at 0.76, best among our TCGA-trained readers. Per-laboratory score normalisation and a laboratory's own slides improve it further on a new site. Without a GPU our reader needs 5-6 s per slide. It serves as a research-use pre-read in a pathology platform, where it proposes a probability and a call beside IHC and helps prioritise ISH for equivocal cases. Weights, per-slide predictions and the data behind every figure are public at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents a 22M-parameter reader that scores HER2 status from routine H&E slides, trained by self-supervision and distillation, which ranks first of 7 encoders on external validation and runs without a GPU at 5 to 6 s per slide. It is deployed as a research-use pre-read in a pathology platform.
AI.motivation: HER2 therapy decisions rely on IHC scoring, with ISH needed for equivocal IHC 2+ tumours, and a low-cost H&E-based reader could serve as a baseline for pathologists and help prioritise ISH.
AI.method: A ViT-S/16 tile encoder was trained on public TCGA slides by self-supervision, distillation from H-optimus-0 and two rounds of JEPA refinement; five cross-validated attention-based slide classifiers average their probabilities, and the operating point is fixed on training data. The team also rebuilt PathBench's encoder benchmark on public cohorts.
AI.result: Under a paired ten-seed protocol the reader ranks first of 7 on external validation from TCGA-BRCA to Yale-HER2 (AUC 0.812), level with readers on encoders 4 and 50 times larger; on three external hospitals it reaches AUC 0.82 on Yale-HER2, 0.75 on HEROHE and 0.63 on BCNB biopsies, and among 85 IHC 2+ HEROHE cases it ranks ISH-amplified above non-amplified tumours at 0.76.
AI.conclusion: The reader is a credible baseline for HER2 pre-reading and ISH prioritisation, with per-laboratory score normalisation and local slides improving it further at a new site, and its weights and per-slide predictions are public.

title: Intervention-Conditioned Counterfactual Human Digital Twin Generator
summary: Chronic diseases evolve through long, heterogeneous trajectories shaped by interacting mediators, confounders, and treatment histories. Estimating long-term patient trajectories under alternative interventions is essential for in silico clinical trial design. However, most existing models overlook irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator dependencies, both of which are crucial for reliable long-term longitudinal prediction. Moreover, these models typically focus on outcome prediction rather than generating complete patient-state trajectories. To address these challenges, we propose CHDT, an intervention-conditioned Human Digital Twin generator under standard identification assumptions for multimodal longitudinal trajectory estimation. Its main empirical advantage arises from explicit modeling of irregular visit intervals, while cross-mediator refinement provides additional gains in selected intervention-conditioned settings. Across real-world ADNI and simulator-generated ALPACA cohorts, CHDT shows improved long-horizon patient-state fidelity relative to competing baselines. Ablation results indicate that irregular-time conditioning provides the primary empirical gain, and cross-mediator refinement provides additional improvements.

AI.tldr: Introduces CHDT, an intervention-conditioned generator of human digital twins that models irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator dependencies to produce long-horizon patient-state trajectories. It improves trajectory fidelity on the ADNI and ALPACA cohorts.
AI.motivation: Chronic disease trajectories are shaped by interacting mediators, confounders and treatment histories, but existing models overlook irregular visit intervals and cross-mediator dependencies and focus on outcome prediction rather than full patient-state trajectories.
AI.method: CHDT is an intervention-conditioned generator, under standard identification assumptions, for multimodal longitudinal trajectory estimation, with explicit modelling of irregular visit intervals and a cross-mediator refinement step.
AI.result: Across the real ADNI cohort and the simulator-generated ALPACA cohort, CHDT improves long-horizon patient-state fidelity relative to competing baselines; ablations show that irregular-time conditioning gives the primary gain and cross-mediator refinement adds further improvement in selected intervention-conditioned settings.
AI.conclusion: Modelling irregular visit timing is the main source of gains for long-horizon digital twin generation, with cross-mediator refinement a secondary benefit in some intervention settings.

title: Recycle only when you have to!
summary: AlphaFold 3-like models (e.g., Boltz, Protenix, etc.) have pushed the frontier of protein binder design. This architecture is used both for the generation of binder candidates (e.g., by hallucination or converting these models into backbone or full atom generative models) as well as for the screening of these candidates for valid binders. In this paper, we start from the observation that AlphaFold 3's confidence metrics (ipSAE, ipTM) as well as structural consistency metrics can be predicted directly from the trunk even at early recycling. Because our proposed predictor is cheap, differentiable, and available at every cycle, it can be used in two distinct ways: as a decision signal to wisely spend the recycling budget for screening and as an objective for hallucination-based design. We show that both applications lead to increased performance at significantly reduced computational cost.

AI.tldr: Shows that AlphaFold 3-style confidence metrics, such as ipSAE and ipTM, can be predicted from the trunk at early recycling steps, and uses this cheap predictor both to decide where to spend the recycling budget and as a design objective. Both uses improve performance at reduced cost.
AI.motivation: Models such as Boltz and Protenix are used both to generate and to screen protein binder candidates, and recycling is computationally expensive.
AI.method: A predictor of ipSAE, ipTM and structural consistency metrics is built from the trunk at early recycling steps; it is cheap, differentiable and available at every cycle, and it serves as a decision signal for screening and as an objective for hallucination-based design.
AI.result: Both applications increase performance while significantly reducing computational cost; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Early, trunk-based confidence prediction lets the recycling budget be spent selectively in binder screening and design.

title: VitisGP: Multi-Task Benchmark for Genotype to Phenotype Grapevine Prediction
summary: As climate change reshapes grape-growing conditions, predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation is increasingly important for identifying and breeding cultivars suited to emerging environmental pressures. Existing research on the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship using machine learning has often focused on individual traits, isolated regions, or a limited set of predictive models. We introduce VitisGP, a multi-phenotype curated dataset, integrating genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks spanning sommelier-curated aroma traits (N=11), botanical traits (N=14) and wine color---across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars. We employ VitisGP to benchmark phenotype prediction, comparing machine-learning models with differing inductive biases---L2-regularized logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models, providing the first systematic comparison of this breadth on harmonized grapevine data. Across the benchmark, CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696 across 26 tasks), although model performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and color traits showing stronger predictability than agronomic characteristics. VitisGP provides the community with a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.

AI.tldr: Introduces VitisGP, a curated multi-phenotype benchmark linking genome-wide SNP data to 26 grapevine phenotype prediction tasks across 1,197 cultivars, and finds CatBoost strongest overall with a macro-average AUROC of 0.696.
AI.motivation: Existing machine-learning studies of the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship focus on individual traits, isolated regions or a limited set of models, which constrains breeding for climate-relevant traits.
AI.method: SNP data are paired with 26 tasks covering sommelier-curated aroma traits (11), botanical traits (14) and wine colour across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars, and six model families are compared: L2-regularised logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models.
AI.result: CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance with a macro-average AUROC of 0.696 across the 26 tasks; performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and colour traits more predictable than agronomic characteristics.
AI.conclusion: VitisGP gives the community a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and for screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.

title: Dual-Corrected Stochastic Block Model ($\text{DC}^2\text{SBM}$): A Generalized Structure Detection Method for Attributed Networks
summary: Community detection in attributed networks is one of the core tasks of complex network analysis. The stochastic block model (SBM) and its variants are able to detect generalized network structures such as assortative, disassortative and mixed structures. However, existing generative methods either ignore node heterogeneity, or characterize node activity in the topological and attribute dimensions by one and the same factor, making it difficult to correctly model node activity when the two kinds of activity are decoupled. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Corrected Stochastic Block Model ($\text{DC}^2\text{SBM}$), which introduces independent correction factors---a topological degree factor and an attribute abundance factor---into the link-generation and attribute-generation channels, respectively, thereby effectively decoupling node activity from membership inference, and which further introduces a global scaling parameter to resolve the mismatch between the normalization constraints and the network scale. The model is inferred by the expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm, and the newly introduced factors cancel out completely in the posterior computation, so that no additional computational cost is incurred. Experiments on synthetic and real attributed networks show that DC^2SBM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in community detection accuracy, with an especially pronounced advantage when the topological signal is weak. The two correction factors can be recovered independently from their respective channels without cross-talk. Analytical as well as controlled experiments further demonstrate that modeling with a single shared factor fails when the two kinds of activity are decoupled---a regime that is prevalent in real networks---thereby validating the necessity of dual independent correction.

AI.tldr: Proposes DC^2SBM, a stochastic block model with independent topological-degree and attribute-abundance correction factors, which improves community detection in attributed networks, especially when the topological signal is weak.
AI.motivation: Existing generative SBM variants either ignore node heterogeneity or use one shared factor for both topological and attribute activity, which fails when the two kinds of node activity are decoupled, a regime common in real networks.
AI.method: Independent correction factors, a topological degree factor and an attribute abundance factor, enter the link-generation and attribute-generation channels respectively, and a global scaling parameter resolves the mismatch between normalisation constraints and network scale; inference uses EM, and the new factors cancel in the posterior.
AI.result: On synthetic and real attributed networks DC^2SBM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in community detection accuracy, with an especially pronounced advantage when the topological signal is weak; the two correction factors are recovered independently without cross-talk, and a single shared factor fails when the two activities are decoupled.
AI.conclusion: Dual independent correction is necessary for modelling decoupled node activity in real networks, and it adds no extra computational cost to inference.

title: CausalGrade: Evidence-Guided Causal Graph Scoring with Jev
summary: Evaluating the structural quality of candidate causal graphs when the true causal structure is unknown is an important problem in applying causal discovery results. This paper proposes CausalGrade, a causal graph scoring method based on the probabilistic judgment model Jev. The method jointly provides Jev with evidence of association, conditional dependence, and directionality from observational data and edge probabilities produced by the causal discovery foundation model CDFM. Jev produces probabilistic judgments about direct causal edges, and a graph-level score is obtained by measuring the agreement between the adjacency structure of the graph under evaluation and these edge-level judgments. Across 300 synthetic datasets, the score exhibits a relatively strong negative correlation with structural error in all 20 combinations of four causal discovery algorithms and five variable counts, indicating that higher scores generally correspond to smaller structural errors. In 500 synthetic graph selection tasks, CausalGrade achieves a best-candidate hit rate of 54.4\%, exceeding the 48.4\% achieved by the Self-Compatibility metric \(\kappa_G\), further supporting its ability to discriminate the structural quality of graphs under evaluation.

AI.tldr: CausalGrade scores candidate causal graphs without knowing the true structure by combining observational-data evidence and edge probabilities from a causal discovery foundation model, judged by the Jev model. Across 300 synthetic datasets, higher scores correspond to smaller structural errors, and it picks the best candidate graph more often than the Self-Compatibility metric.
AI.motivation: Evaluating the structural quality of candidate causal graphs is hard when the true causal structure is unknown, which limits how causal discovery results can be applied.
AI.method: CausalGrade gives the Jev probabilistic judgment model evidence of association, conditional dependence and directionality from observational data, together with edge probabilities from the CDFM causal discovery foundation model. Jev produces edge-level judgments, and a graph-level score measures the agreement between the evaluated graph's adjacency structure and these judgments.
AI.result: The score has a relatively strong negative correlation with structural error in all 20 combinations of four causal discovery algorithms and five variable counts across 300 synthetic datasets. In 500 synthetic graph selection tasks it reaches a best-candidate hit rate of 54.4%, against 48.4% for the Self-Compatibility metric (kappa_G).
AI.conclusion: The score discriminates the structural quality of candidate graphs, supporting its use for selecting among causal discovery results when the true structure is unknown.

title: CalibCause: A Quality-Gated, Interpretable and Calibrated Deep Learning Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
summary: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. We propose CalibCause, a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework that combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. We evaluated the framework using 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR, and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing. Evaluation included pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and local grade-threshold adaptation. On the pooled test split, the label-free distilled student achieved quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863 and accuracy of 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters, 52% fewer than its teacher. Across held-out environments, the label-free model achieved mean QWK of 0.741 compared with 0.743 for a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline, while adversarial invariance did not improve cross-site grading accuracy. Refitting grade thresholds using 200 labelled images increased held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621 for the label-free model. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranged from 0.025 to 0.036 across CalibCause variants, and deferring the least confident 20% of images increased student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images. These findings demonstrate that quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression, and calibrated deferral can be integrated without sacrificing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.

AI.tldr: CalibCause is a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework for diabetic retinopathy grading that adds per-expert explanations, image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation and calibrated deferral. Its label-free distilled student stays close to a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline in cross-site performance while using 52% fewer parameters than its teacher.
AI.motivation: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration and interpretability.
AI.method: A quality-gated mixture-of-experts combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. The framework is evaluated on 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing, using pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals and local grade-threshold adaptation.
AI.result: On the pooled test split the label-free distilled student reaches QWK 0.863 and accuracy 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters. Across held-out environments its mean QWK is 0.741, against 0.743 for plain ConvNeXt-Tiny. Refitting grade thresholds with 200 labelled images raises held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranges from 0.025 to 0.036, and deferring the least confident 20% raises student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images.
AI.conclusion: Quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression and calibrated deferral can be combined without losing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.

title: FGSM Attack Transferability from Simulation to Quantum Hardware in Network Intrusion Detection
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI), 13-16 December 2026, Nottingham, UK. Code: this https URL
summary: Quantum computers are now available through cloud platforms, and recent work has proposed using them to detect network intrusions. It is not yet clear how easily such systems can be attacked. We train a hybrid variational quantum classifier (VQC) on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and test it against two attacks: label flipping during training and FGSM evasion at prediction time. We run the tests in simulation and on IBM hardware, the Fez superconducting processor (Heron r2). We find that two models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how easily they are attacked. A model that decides with little confidence loses half its detections to a very small change in the input, while a model trained to decide with more confidence needs a much larger change before it fails. Attacks built in simulation against the more confident model also work on real hardware, and the device classifies every unaltered attack sample correctly. Simulated device noise does not reduce accuracy, but it does reduce the model's confidence and makes attacks easier, so accuracy alone does not show how exposed a model is. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed. These results show that device noise should not be treated as a defense and that reported weaknesses in these classifiers depend partly on how they were trained.

AI.tldr: A hybrid variational quantum classifier for network intrusion detection can be attacked with FGSM evasion and label flipping, and attacks built in simulation transfer to IBM Fez hardware. Accuracy alone does not show how exposed a model is, because simulated device noise lowers confidence and makes attacks easier without changing accuracy.
AI.motivation: It is not yet clear how easily quantum-computer-based intrusion detectors can be attacked, even though such systems have recently been proposed and cloud quantum hardware is available.
AI.method: A hybrid variational quantum classifier is trained on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and tested against label flipping during training and FGSM evasion at prediction time. The tests run in simulation and on the IBM Fez superconducting processor (Heron r2).
AI.result: Two models with similar accuracy differ greatly in how easily they are attacked. A low-confidence model loses half its detections to a very small input change, while a more confidently trained model needs a much larger change. Attacks built in simulation against the confident model also work on hardware, which classifies every unaltered attack sample correctly. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed.
AI.conclusion: Device noise should not be treated as a defense, and reported weaknesses of these classifiers depend partly on how they were trained.

title: The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
summary: Learning a shared subspace in multitask learning is an important statistical problem, yet exact rates remain poorly understood in many of the formal settings considered in the literature. To address this gap, which arises from limitations of existing upper-bound techniques, we propose a general multitask lemma. The lemma provides sufficient conditions for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings, in the form of geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators. We subsequently show that the multitask lemma yields sharp minimax rates---previously unknown---for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates matching up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a general multitask lemma that gives geometric sufficient conditions for fast shared-subspace estimation, and uses it to obtain sharp minimax rates for linear regression and classification. For additive-noise regression the rates match up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: Exact rates for learning a shared subspace in multitask learning remain poorly understood, and limitations of existing upper-bound techniques leave this gap open.
AI.method: A general multitask lemma gives sufficient conditions, stated as geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators, for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings.
AI.result: The lemma yields sharp minimax rates, previously unknown, for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates that match up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.
AI.conclusion: The lemma gives a unified route to sharp rates for shared subspace estimation in settings where earlier upper-bound techniques fell short.

title: PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management
summary: Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22--55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy--utility--autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.

AI.tldr: PrivacyFlow is a defense for LLM agents that plans each data disclosure with contextual integrity reasoning before execution, and the paper introduces agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks. Across six models it raises the share of task sequences completed without a detected privacy violation by 22 to 55 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM agents working on personal data over multi-step workflows often leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Contextual Integrity formalises this problem, but existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalise it for realistic multi-step sequences in evolving environments.
AI.method: PrivacyFlow separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1). Before execution it traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimised plan, blocks it, or consults the user. The benchmark has 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets.
AI.result: PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures across six models and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22 to 55 percentage points. Letting it prompt the user under uncertainty raises authorised task completion, but shifts decision effort back to the user.
AI.conclusion: Proactive contextual integrity reasoning can substantially improve agent privacy, and the privacy-utility-autonomy tradeoff it reveals merits further study.

title: INLA for Adaptive UAV Sampling of Radio Environment Maps in IoT Networks: Prior Width Governs Accuracy and Calibration
summary: We study adaptive UAV sampling for radio environment map (REM) construction from non-Gaussian IoT observations. Integrated nested Laplace approximation(INLA) updates a Matérn GMRF posterior, with waypoints selected by entropy pre-screening and Sherman--Morrison lookahead over the reachable set. We show that the likelihood-induced Skew-Normal correction has a sextic entropy effect, explaining its limited influence on waypoint selection. Across 19 retained ray-traced windows,Random and lawnmower sampling cost a median 18.0\% and 14.0\% more residual NMSE than posterior-informed sampling, equivalently reductions of 15.3\% and 12.3\% when referred to those baselines, while differences among informative rules remain unresolved. Widening the prior shadowing standard deviation from 6.0 to 10.025\,dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage, with monotone improvement over a 4--16\,dB sweep on this corpus and no observed turning point, although overconfidence persists. Online width estimation from the UAV's own counts yields about 6.5\,dB without recovering the gain. Across 30 measured LoRaWAN propagation windows paired with simulated counts and scored only on received cells, the margin over non-adaptive sampling reproduces, the training-derived width minimizes the tested interval score, and GP-UCB has nominally $3$--$5\%$ lower NMSE. The results show substantial, corpus-dependent sensitivity to prior specification, while fine differences among acquisition rules have limited or unresolved effects, the preferred width depends on the corpus, scored cells and model mismatch.

AI.tldr: The paper studies adaptive UAV sampling for radio environment map construction using INLA with a Matern GMRF posterior, and finds that the prior shadowing standard deviation has a larger effect on accuracy and calibration than the choice among informative acquisition rules. Widening the prior from 6.0 to 10.025 dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage.
AI.motivation: Building radio environment maps from non-Gaussian IoT observations requires deciding where the UAV samples, and the paper examines how prior specification and acquisition rules affect the resulting accuracy.
AI.method: INLA updates a Matern GMRF posterior, with waypoints selected by entropy pre-screening and Sherman-Morrison lookahead over the reachable set. The paper also analyses the likelihood-induced Skew-Normal correction, which has a sextic entropy effect that explains its limited influence on waypoint selection.
AI.result: Across 19 retained ray-traced windows, random and lawnmower sampling cost a median 18.0% and 14.0% more residual NMSE than posterior-informed sampling. Widening the shadowing prior from 6.0 to 10.025 dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage, monotonically over a 4 to 16 dB sweep, though overconfidence persists. Online width estimation from the UAV's own counts gives about 6.5 dB without recovering the gain. Across 30 measured LoRaWAN windows the margin over non-adaptive sampling reproduces, and GP-UCB has nominally 3 to 5% lower NMSE.
AI.conclusion: Results are substantially sensitive to prior specification and depend on the corpus, while differences among acquisition rules remain limited or unresolved.

title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Li2SAO adds group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping to a lightweight single-rollout asynchronous RL method, removing the need for a closed-source pretrained value model. It catches up with or surpasses GRPO early in training and raises the later performance ceiling.
AI.motivation: Single-rollout asynchronous optimization (SAO) suits asynchronous RL for LLMs, but it relies on a closed-source value model, and the open reproduction LiSAO lags GRPO early in training because its value model is not yet well trained.
AI.method: Li2SAO (Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization) uses group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping. While the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic; training then switches to single-rollout GAE.
AI.result: GRPO outperforms LiSAO on single-turn reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on multi-turn agentic tasks. Li2SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling.
AI.conclusion: Group-relative bootstrapping lets single-rollout asynchronous RL match or beat GRPO without a pretrained value model, supporting its use for LLM post-training.

title: Model-Agnostic Search for New Physics in the Presence of Imperfect Background by Smearing the Data
summary: In the search for new particles in high-energy physics, it is necessary to first define the signal region (SR) enriched in signal events, and then compare events in this region with the expected background distribution. While most existing search methods rely on prior domain knowledge of either the signal or the background, there has been less effort to relax both assumptions simultaneously, as methods that weaken one assumption typically rely on strong knowledge of the other. We propose Model-Agnostic Search with Smearing and Imperfect Background (MASSIB), a method that addresses this challenge by learning the density ratio of events relative to a misspecified background distribution using modern tools from machine learning, and defining the SR as the region with high density ratio. Recognizing that a naive application of this idea introduces significant bias in background estimation when interpolating from the control region to the SR, MASSIB mitigates this issue by introducing a "smeared" density ratio, which can be learned efficiently through data-level manipulation and used to define an SR that allows for accurate background estimation. By applying it to various types of simulated Large Hadron Collider (LHC) events with realistic background mismodeling, we demonstrate that MASSIB identifies a data-driven SR that achieves high signal concentration consistently across different types of signals while avoiding bias in background estimation. The method does this without making strong assumptions about either the signal or background distribution. We then show that this robustness extends to the validity and strong statistical power of the resulting hypothesis tests for signal detection, demonstrating the potential of this approach for future model-agnostic searches at the LHC.

AI.tldr: MASSIB is a model-agnostic search for new physics that defines the signal region by a smeared density ratio learned relative to an imperfect background, avoiding bias in background estimation. On simulated LHC events with realistic background mismodelling it achieves high signal concentration and valid, powerful hypothesis tests.
AI.motivation: Existing search methods rely on prior knowledge of either the signal or the background, and methods that relax one assumption typically depend strongly on the other. A naive density-ratio signal region also biases background estimation when interpolating from the control region.
AI.method: MASSIB learns the density ratio of events relative to a misspecified background distribution with modern machine learning and defines the signal region as the region of high density ratio. It introduces a smeared density ratio, learned through data-level manipulation, to correct the bias when interpolating from the control region to the signal region.
AI.result: Applied to various types of simulated LHC events with realistic background mismodelling, MASSIB identifies a data-driven signal region with high signal concentration across signal types while avoiding bias in background estimation. The resulting hypothesis tests show validity and strong statistical power.
AI.conclusion: The approach makes no strong assumptions about either the signal or the background distribution, and shows potential for future model-agnostic searches at the LHC.

title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
summary: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision.
