AI.method: Three outcome comparison criteria extract preferences from rollouts started at the same state and leave comparisons unresolved when evidence is insufficient or conflicting; a state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from these preferences and guides search without online rollouts; non-dominated heuristic action supervision keeps the solver-selected action as a target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences.
AI.result: SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-derived preferences, with unresolved comparisons left open rather than forced into a predefined scalar ordering, provide a usable learning signal for CDCL branching.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

AI.tldr: ASTC is a training-free method that uses the model's own recurrent dynamics in hybrid GDN-attention to carry absorbed context forward as soft tokens while keeping exact values as hard tokens, matching agent accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer attention pairs.
AI.motivation: Growing interaction contexts raise computation cost and obscure decision-relevant evidence, while trained external compressors rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences that may misalign with the LLM's evolving representation and are lossy.
AI.method: ASTC uses the native recurrent dynamics of the hybrid Gated Delta Network attention to determine which information is already absorbed, carries it forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens, and yields a compact sequence with reusable KV caches.
AI.result: On long-horizon tasks ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task.
AI.conclusion: Agentic soft tokens offer a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

title: Operon-S1: a fast decision controller for long-horizon biomedical agents
comment: 40 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables, 5 Extended Data figures, 6 Extended Data tables
summary: Language-model agents now carry out long scientific work in biology, but their judgements about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and stopping are made inside the reasoning that does the work, where they cannot be measured, replaced or improved on their own. Here we present Operon-S1, a fast decision system, a System 1 for the agent, that separates judging from doing. A decision harness poses the agent's recurring judgements as closed questions at 13 decision points and acts only through fixed messages that never contain an answer, so any model that answers the questions can serve as the judge. Across seven life-science benchmarks, a local decision model took over these judgements in 0.6 s at the median for an in-loop request on CPU at no request cost, with no measurable change in the agent's score on five of six benchmarks, whereas the general language model that drives the agent, asked the same questions, accounted for 8.0% to 35.2% of task cost. Every decision is recorded with its consequence. Retraining on labels from task construction, verifiers or execution raised decision accuracy on every question in each of three trained versions, and a new version enters service only through a promotion gate. Task-level results in this study use the public checkpoint. The same closed decisions serve wet-laboratory protocol troubleshooting and the design of a germline target enrichment panel. Like the regulator of an operon, which switches genes on and off without making their products, Operon-S1 steers the agent without doing its work, and makes the agent's judgements a layer that can be measured, replaced and trained.

AI.tldr: Operon-S1 is a fast decision controller that poses an agent's recurring judgements as closed questions answered by a local model, which took these decisions in 0.6 s at the median on CPU at no request cost, with no measurable score change on five of six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Judgements about conventions, skills, errors, evidence and stopping are made inside the agent's reasoning, where they cannot be measured, replaced or improved on their own.
AI.method: A decision harness poses judgements as closed questions at 13 decision points and acts only through fixed messages that never contain an answer, so any model that answers the questions can serve as judge; every decision is recorded with its consequence, and retrained versions enter service only through a promotion gate.
AI.result: Across seven life-science benchmarks the local decision model took over the judgements, whereas the general language model driving the agent accounted for 8.0% to 35.2% of task cost when asked the same questions; retraining on labels from task construction, verifiers or execution raised decision accuracy on every question in each of three trained versions.
AI.conclusion: Separating judging from doing makes the agent's judgements a layer that can be measured, replaced and trained, and the same closed decisions serve wet-laboratory protocol troubleshooting and germline target enrichment panel design.

title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. To address this, model embeddings compress each model into a fixed-length vector from which many properties can be predicted. Existing methods, such as EmbedLLM, build these vectors from correctness patterns and question features, and often need large probe batteries to do so. However, many behaviors that are important when choosing a model, such as its verbosity, safety and style, show up more in how it answers than in whether it is correct. We introduce BULLPEN (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings), a framework that extends EmbedLLM in three ways. First, BULLPEN organizes the downstream tasks that prior work uses and adds 20 task benchmarks we built on behavior, style and provenance. Second, it is the first framework to read a model's own answer text jointly with its correctness and the question text. Third, it encodes models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool. Across 260 open-weight models, our answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder. Our encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from only 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute of the full question pool), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83% with the same 400 questions. Because these embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioral auditing and low-cost profiling, and could extend to API-only models. Code and data: this https URL

AI.tldr: BULLPEN encodes LLMs into profile vectors from a few hundred questions by reading answer text jointly with correctness and question text, improving prediction of behavioural properties such as verbosity, safety and style over the best prior encoder.
AI.motivation: Choosing an LLM requires knowing properties like verbosity, safety and style that show up more in how a model answers than in whether it is correct, while existing EmbedLLM-style embeddings rely on correctness patterns and large probe batteries.
AI.method: BULLPEN extends EmbedLLM by organising the downstream tasks and adding 20 new behaviour, style and provenance benchmarks, by being the first framework to read answer text jointly with correctness and question text, and by encoding models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool.
AI.result: Across 260 open-weight models the answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder; encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83%.
AI.conclusion: Because the embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioural auditing and low-cost profiling and could extend to API-only models.

title: Riemannian Optimization on Unknown Manifolds via Stochastic Proximal Refinement
summary: We study Riemannian optimization on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples. The central challenge is to turn feasible samples into optimization steps, i.e., the samples are drawn from the unknown feasible manifold, but do not directly provide the tangent spaces, projections, or retractions required by classic Riemannian methods. Moreover, regions with low objective values may be sparsely represented in the data, so directly sampling from a distribution fitted to these observations can require many draws to find better feasible solutions. We introduce Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds (PRISM), which turns feasible-sample access into an iterative optimization procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. Theoretically, we show that PRISM recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, leading to provable objective descent, feasibility (manifold adherence), and convergence toward first-order stationarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through synthetic experiments illustrating its geometric properties and applications to data-driven building control and diverse real world optimization tasks, highlighting its potential as a general framework for data-driven optimization across scientific and engineering domains.

AI.tldr: PRISM performs optimisation on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples, repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution around the current iterate, with provable objective descent, feasibility and convergence to first-order stationarity.
AI.motivation: Classic Riemannian methods need tangent spaces, projections or retractions that feasible samples do not provide, and low-objective regions may be sparsely represented in the data, so sampling directly from a fitted distribution can require many draws.
AI.method: Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds turns feasible-sample access into an iterative procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate.
AI.result: PRISM is shown to recover the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, with provable objective descent, manifold adherence and convergence toward first-order stationarity; synthetic experiments illustrate its geometry, and applications include data-driven building control and diverse real-world optimisation tasks.
AI.conclusion: PRISM is positioned as a general framework for data-driven optimisation across scientific and engineering domains.

title: DUGO: Dual-Scale Gaussian Memory for Online Temporal Action Localization in Egocentric Procedural Videos
comment: This paper has been accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026)
summary: Online Temporal Action Localization (OnTAL) aims to detect and localize action instances from untrimmed streaming videos in real time. Unlike offline approaches, OnTAL models have no access to future frames and cannot go back and refine earlier predictions, which makes the task considerably harder given the strict real-time constraints and narrow temporal window available. Most existing OnTAL methods lean on either brief anchor-based context or a single-scale memory of past frames, which limits how well they can capture actions unfolding across multiple time scales or requiring long-range reasoning in Procedural Videos. To address these gaps, we present DUGO (Dual-Scale Encoding and Gaussian Memory Online), a new OnTAL framework that jointly models local motion dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies. At its core, DUGO uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder, pairing depth-wise local representations with global self-attention so it can pick up both fine-grained temporal patterns and broader contextual cues. We also introduce a Gaussian Memory Bank, which represents action memory as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes, allowing for richer temporal memory through gated cross-attention applied at both the encoder and anchor-query stages. Extensive experiments on procedural egocentric datasets (EGTEA, EPIC-Kitchens-100) demonstrate that DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance while also providing substantial improvements on non-egocentric benchmarks such as Muses. The project page is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: DUGO is an online temporal action localization framework for streaming videos that jointly models local motion and long-range dependencies with a dual-scale encoder and a Gaussian memory bank. It reports state-of-the-art results on procedural egocentric datasets and substantial gains on the non-egocentric Muses benchmark.
AI.motivation: Online action localization must decide from past frames only under strict real-time limits, and existing methods rely on brief anchor-based context or single-scale memory, which cannot capture actions across multiple time scales or long-range reasoning in procedural videos.
AI.method: A Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder pairs depth-wise local representations with global self-attention, and a Gaussian Memory Bank stores actions as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes that are read through gated cross-attention at the encoder and anchor-query stages.
AI.result: DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance on EGTEA and EPIC-Kitchens-100 and substantial improvements on Muses, a non-egocentric benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modelling local dynamics and long-range dependencies with a probabilistic memory is effective for online localization in both egocentric procedural videos and general videos.

title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation
summary: Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different this http URL propose a residualanchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning this http URL evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a residual-anchor Neural SDE that splits a conditional financial time-series target into a learned context-dependent anchor and a stochastic residual. On real financial series it generates plausible conditional paths with competitive point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Directly modelling the target state in conditional Neural SDEs is unstable when the target and the conditioning variables have strong level dependence, when training data are limited, or when the variables differ in nature.
AI.method: The target is decomposed into a learned conditional anchor that captures the context-dependent baseline and a stochastic residual modelled by a Neural SDE with learnable drift and diffusion, which generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning.
AI.result: On real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model, the model generates plausible conditional paths, maintains competitive point accuracy and provides calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: Separating a conditional baseline from stochastic residual dynamics makes conditional path generation more stable and useful for financial scenario modelling with uncertainty.

title: SACQ: Structure-Aware Codebook Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable capable robot behavior, but their large memory footprint limits deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Weight quantization is a natural remedy, yet post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes inherited from large language models degrade when applied to VLAs at ultra-low precision. Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions. We introduce SACQ, an ultra- low-bit weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for VLAs. SACQ combines (1) structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic metrics that reflect input statistics and downstream sensitivity; (2) action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in final-action error as individual layers are compressed; and (3) two-stage post-quantization refinement that reassigns codeword indices with second-order error compensation and calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the decoded action. Using GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83x. With INT8 activation quantization and low-precision attention, it retains 93.55% success while running 1.51x faster than BF16. On SimplER, SACQ further achieves 63.76% and 52.27% success under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation at 2 bits per language/action weight, compared to 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16, respectively.

AI.tldr: SACQ is an ultra-low-bit, weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for Vision-Language-Action models. Applied to GR00T N1.7 it keeps 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83x.
AI.motivation: VLA models have large memory footprints that limit deployment on resource-constrained robots, and post-training quantization recipes inherited from large language models degrade at ultra-low precision because they ignore the structure of downstream operations and the effect of precision on final actions.
AI.method: SACQ combines structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic metrics, action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in final-action error when layers are compressed, and two-stage post-quantization refinement with second-order error compensation and codebook and row-group scale calibration against the decoded action.
AI.result: With GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight and reduces memory 4.83x; with INT8 activation quantization and low-precision attention it retains 93.55% success while running 1.51x faster than BF16. On SimplER it reaches 63.76% and 52.27% success under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation at 2 bits, compared with 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16.
AI.conclusion: Action-aware, structure-aware codebook quantization can push VLAs to about 1.5 to 2 bits per weight while staying close to full-precision success, which makes deployment on constrained robotic platforms more feasible.

title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
summary: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. We designed a large language model (LLM)-based visit preparation agent to guide patients before an appointment by gathering clinical context, setting visit expectations, providing relevant health information, building a prioritized list of questions for their clinician, and generating a summary. In a prospective consented randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults held 866 health-related conversations with the visit preparation agent (standard or concise variant) or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. The visit preparation agent significantly outperformed the control across blinded clinician evaluations and patient self-reports. In clinician reviews of completed sessions (n = 272), the agent achieved a 16.6% higher rate of comprehensive preparation (67.2% vs. 50.6%; P < 0.05) and an 8.5% higher rate of alignment with patients' health context (98.9% vs. 90.4%; P < 0.01), while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness across all study arms. Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed 16.8% higher visit preparedness (73.8% vs. 57.0%; P < 0.01), 14.3% higher confidence in knowing what to ask (81.4% vs. 67.1%; P < 0.01), and 12.0% higher overall satisfaction (74.0% vs. 62.0%; P < 0.05). Clinician and participant metrics were not significantly correlated, indicating that expert review and patient self-assessment capture complementary dimensions of patient-facing AI. These findings suggest that LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and motivate future studies on in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.

AI.tldr: A prospective randomized study of 802 US adults found that an LLM-based visit preparation agent outperformed a minimally prompted control chatbot on clinician-rated and patient-reported measures of preparation, while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness.
AI.motivation: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unprepared, and general-purpose AI chatbots are widely used for preparation, yet whether conversational AI actually improves visit readiness was unclear.
AI.method: An LLM-based visit preparation agent gathers clinical context, sets visit expectations, provides relevant health information, builds a prioritized question list and generates a summary, and was compared in a consented randomized study in the Google Health app against a control chatbot built on the same LLM, using standard and concise agent variants.
AI.result: Across 866 health-related conversations, clinician reviews (n = 272) showed comprehensive preparation at 67.2% versus 50.6% (P < 0.05) and alignment with patient health context at 98.9% versus 90.4% (P < 0.01). Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed preparedness at 73.8% versus 57.0%, confidence in knowing what to ask at 81.4% versus 67.1%, and satisfaction at 74.0% versus 62.0%. Clinician and patient metrics were not significantly correlated.
AI.conclusion: LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and future studies should test in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.

title: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
comment: Interpretability as a Science Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. For this, we patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the unmodified base model, and vice versa. Our results show that for some behaviors, like responding in German or emergent misalignment, patching the KV cache can indeed transfer them from the fine-tuned to the base model. Correspondingly, patching the KV cache from base to fine-tune can partially or fully remove fine-tuned behavior. Furthermore, we find that the effect of patching grows with how much of the KV cache is patched and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.

AI.tldr: The paper patches the KV cache between a LoRA fine-tuned model and its unmodified base model to locate where fine-tuned behaviours arise. Patching transfers some behaviours, such as responding in German and emergent misalignment, and its effect concentrates at a few pivotal positions, notably system-prompt and chat-template tokens.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether a fine-tuned behaviour appears only while the answer tokens are generated or whether altered processing of earlier tokens through the attention mechanism causes it.
AI.method: The KV cache of a LoRA fine-tuned model is patched into the base model and vice versa, and the transfer is measured as a function of how much of the cache is patched and at which positions.
AI.result: For some behaviours, including responding in German and emergent misalignment, patching the fine-tuned cache transfers the behaviour to the base model, and patching base into fine-tuned partially or fully removes it. The effect grows with the patched fraction of the cache and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.
AI.conclusion: Part of a fine-tuned behaviour is instantiated in the cached keys and values of earlier tokens rather than only in answer-token generation, and a small set of structural tokens carries much of this effect.

title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
summary: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer), and maintains this lead on two out-of-distribution benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that DAPS premises improve theorem proving on miniF2F and IMO-ProofBench. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: DAPS is a dependency-aware premise selector for Lean 4 theorem proving, trained on dependency data from 53 Lean Blueprint projects and typed Mathlib4 dependencies. It reaches mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on Mathlib4-Heldout, 11.41 points above LeanHammer, and its premises improve proving on miniF2F and IMO-ProofBench.
AI.motivation: Existing neural premise selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, which skews retrieval toward popular foundational lemmas, ranks pairs in isolation and degrades on out-of-distribution queries, so newly contributed research-level premises are hard to leverage.
AI.method: The authors mine 3,805 manually curated informal and formal nodes from 53 Lean Blueprint projects and extract comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies, then train DAPS with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure.
AI.result: DAPS reaches mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer) and maintains this lead on two out-of-distribution benchmarks; its premises further improve theorem proving on miniF2F and IMO-ProofBench.
AI.conclusion: Restoring dependency structure to both the training data and the model yields better premise retrieval and proving, particularly for rare research-level lemmas absent from Mathlib4.

title: DeepWeave: Weaving Neural and Symbolic Evidence for ML-Based Network Intrusion Detection System
summary: Machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems can recognize complex traffic patterns, but often require substantial labelled attack data, degrade under deployment shift, and provide limited evidence for analysts. We present DeepWeave, a probabilistic neuro-symbolic Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) that makes logic an integral part of detection. DeepWeave automatically constructs and validates interpretable rules, represents neural predictions as probabilistic predicates, and reconciles both evidence sources through explicit coupling policies over packet-, flow-, and hybrid-views. The resulting proofs provide intrinsic explanations for rule-supported alerts. Across multiple datasets, DeepWeave improves low-data detection, false-positive control, transferability, and robustness. With only 50 labelled packet observations per attack class, it improves macro-F1 from 0.632 to 0.924 and reduces the attack false-positive rate from 0.075 to 0.008 over the matched neural baseline. Its proofs are also more stable than post-hoc neural attributions, while batched inference keeps probabilistic reasoning practical. These results demonstrate label-efficient, adaptable, and inspectable neuro-symbolic intrusion detection.

AI.tldr: DeepWeave is a probabilistic neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that automatically builds validated logical rules and couples them with neural predictions. With only 50 labelled packet observations per attack class it raises macro-F1 from 0.632 to 0.924 over the matched neural baseline.
AI.motivation: Machine learning based intrusion detection systems need substantial labelled attack data, degrade under deployment shift and give analysts limited evidence for their alerts.
AI.method: DeepWeave constructs and validates interpretable rules, represents neural predictions as probabilistic predicates, and reconciles both sources through explicit coupling policies over packet, flow and hybrid views, so that the resulting proofs explain rule-supported alerts.
AI.result: With 50 labelled packet observations per attack class, macro-F1 improves from 0.632 to 0.924 and the attack false-positive rate falls from 0.075 to 0.008 relative to the matched neural baseline. Across datasets it improves low-data detection, false-positive control, transferability and robustness, and its proofs are more stable than post-hoc neural attributions.
AI.conclusion: Making logic an integral part of detection gives label-efficient, adaptable and inspectable intrusion detection, and batched inference keeps the probabilistic reasoning practical.

title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
comment: 21 pages, 8 figures. Code: this https URL ; Gemma demo: this https URL . Links to all four demos are included in the paper
summary: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.

AI.tldr: BYOD is a LoRA-only recipe that converts autoregressive language models into diffusion language models, covering Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B and Ministral 8B, including the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The conversions retain substantial parent knowledge but lag in open-generation quality at low NFE budgets.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models permit parallel token updates, flexible generation and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning.
AI.method: A generalizable recipe with no architecture-specific tuning trains LoRA adapters comprising 4.1% to 5.8% of final parameters while all base-model parameters stay frozen, using 25,000 iterations and at most 102.4M tokens per conversion.
AI.result: Each conversion takes 3.1 to 4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. BYOD-Gemma reaches 50.6% average accuracy on a nine-task evaluation, compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. At 128 tokens in 64 steps, BYOD perplexity is 8.3 to 11.1, versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2 to 3.0 for the AR parents.
AI.conclusion: BYOD offers a practical route to extend diffusion generation to other existing model families, and efficient conversion must next close the gap in open-generation quality at low NFE budgets.

title: Reliability-Weighted Direct Preference Optimization: Penalized Weights for Robust Preference Learning
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats every reported comparison as correct, yet preference data contain reversed, tied or otherwise noisy comparisons. RW-DPO gives each comparison an unknown reliability weight $w_i\in[0,1]$ that enters the likelihood linearly -- DPO is $w\equiv1$, a reversed comparison $w_i=0$ -- and estimates the weights jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty on $-\log w_i$. The penalty keeps every comparison the model agrees with at exactly $w_i=1$ and acts only on those it contradicts, through closed-form weight updates at negligible cost over DPO. We prove that recovering all flipped comparisons from a single annotation per comparison requires margins of order $\log n$. Furthermore, in a linear-index model, starting from an initial fit pointing in the correct direction, our estimator jointly consistently recovers the preference direction and weights, as well as identifies the flipped comparisons above this margin scale, even when a fixed fraction of comparisons is flipped. In simulations RW-DPO has the lowest average estimation error among DPO, noise-rate corrections and recent robust methods, with far more precise flags than recent label-correction methods. In DPO fine-tuning of a language model with 10-30% flipped labels, its win rate does not fall as the flip rate grows and exceeds that of DPO trained on clean labels, matching the strongest recent method with corrections concentrated on the flipped labels.

AI.tldr: RW-DPO extends Direct Preference Optimization with per-comparison reliability weights estimated jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty, so that flipped comparisons are down-weighted. In language model fine-tuning with 10% to 30% flipped labels its win rate does not fall as the flip rate grows.
AI.motivation: DPO treats every reported comparison as correct, although preference data contain reversed, tied or otherwise noisy comparisons.
AI.method: Each comparison receives an unknown reliability weight in [0,1] that enters the likelihood linearly, with DPO recovered when all weights equal 1 and a reversed comparison receiving weight 0; the weights are estimated jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty on minus log w, which keeps agreeing comparisons at weight 1 and acts only on contradicted ones through closed-form updates.
AI.result: The authors prove that recovering all flipped comparisons from one annotation per comparison requires margins of order log n, and in a linear-index model their estimator jointly and consistently recovers the preference direction and the weights. In simulations RW-DPO has the lowest average estimation error among DPO, noise-rate corrections and recent robust methods, and with 10% to 30% flipped labels its win rate exceeds that of DPO trained on clean labels.
AI.conclusion: Penalized reliability weighting gives a low-cost, theoretically grounded robustification of DPO that matches the strongest recent correction method while flagging flipped labels more precisely.

title: PDE-Residual-Informed Kriging
summary: Physics-informed Gaussian process (GP) methods provide a probabilistic framework for PDE solving. Existing approaches incorporate PDE information in different ways: pointwise conditioning uses the governing equation only at finitely many selected locations, globally constrained GPs restrict the admissible functions to satisfy the PDE exactly, and residual-penalized methods control the PDE mismatch over the whole domain through an additional penalty weight. What is still missing is a GP formulation that directly incorporates global PDE-residual information of the entire domain into its covariance structure, while retaining model flexibility and standard GP conditioning without a separate residual-weight parameter. To solve this issue, this study proposes PDE-residual-informed Kriging (PRIK) based on a PDE-residual kernel. The PDE-residual kernel is constructed by equipping a kernel-section space with an inner product defined by the $L^{2}$ inner product of PDE residuals. This construction makes PRIK yield the posterior mean with minimum integrated squared PDE residual. It also provides direct statistical interpretations: the variance-scale estimate equals the normalized PDE-residual energy (i.e., the integrated squared PDE residual of the posterior mean divided by the number of labeled observations), and the profile likelihood balances this residual energy against model complexity. Under the stated regularity and stability conditions, we establish $H^{2}$-quasi-optimality and convergence rates for the posterior mean, together with a nonasymptotic bound for its PDE-residual norm. We further show that the normalized posterior kernel converges to a variational Green-type kernel and derive a uniform nonasymptotic contraction bound for the posterior variance. Numerical studies provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory and demonstrate the PDE-solving capability of PRIK.

AI.tldr: PRIK is a physics-informed Gaussian process (Kriging) method whose PDE-residual kernel encodes the global PDE residual over the whole domain into the covariance, without a separate residual-weight parameter. The authors establish H2 quasi-optimality and convergence rates and report numerical evidence consistent with the theory.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-informed GP methods use the PDE only at selected points, restrict admissible functions to satisfy the PDE exactly, or penalize the residual with an extra weight, and none directly incorporates whole-domain PDE-residual information into the covariance while keeping standard GP conditioning.
AI.method: The PDE-residual kernel equips a kernel-section space with an inner product given by the L2 inner product of PDE residuals, so the posterior mean minimizes the integrated squared PDE residual, and the variance-scale estimate and profile likelihood admit residual-based interpretations.
AI.result: Under stated regularity and stability conditions the authors establish H2 quasi-optimality and convergence rates for the posterior mean, a nonasymptotic bound on its PDE-residual norm, convergence of the normalized posterior kernel to a variational Green-type kernel, and a uniform nonasymptotic contraction bound for the posterior variance.
AI.conclusion: Building global PDE-residual information into the GP covariance gives a probabilistic PDE solver with interpretable statistics and provable accuracy guarantees.

title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
comment: Main: 12 pages, 6 figures. Supplemental material: 11 pages
summary: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

AI.tldr: The paper uses a machine-learning direct method to find optimal protocols for underdamped stochastic transport with nonlinear Landauer boundary conditions, steering a single-peak position distribution into a double-peak one by acting only on an external potential. The numerical solutions are benchmarked against a perturbative expansion expected to hold in an overdamped limit.
AI.motivation: Optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes are difficult to find, analytical solutions are generally unavailable, and the problem is highly nonlinear, especially with boundary conditions such as those modelling Landauer bit erasure.
AI.method: A direct machine-learning method finds the optimal solution by acting only on a controllable external potential, with the dynamics steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space.
AI.result: The numerical results are benchmarked against a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a practical route to optimal protocols in a nonlinear Landauer-type setting where closed-form solutions are not available, with the perturbative expansion serving as the benchmark.

title: What Carries Architectural Signal? A Code-to-Architecture Mapping Study
summary: Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture. Representations of implementation artifacts can capture code text, dependencies, and directory organization, but predictive gains alone do not establish the contribution of additional graph processing. Dependencies may already be encoded in these representations, while directories may closely match the reference decomposition. We investigate how artifact representations and graph context affect mapping on ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget. We compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations and assess each predictor with and without dependency neighbors. Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), we compare file-level graphs extended with member nodes summarizing each file's program elements, folder nodes, or both, alongside a variant encoding folder paths directly in file representations. We compare folder-aware predictions with a directory rule using the same labeled files. Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical representations on most systems. Additional neighbor aggregation can improve mapping, depending on the predictor and aggregation direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains across the evaluated HGT configurations. However, the directory rule achieves per-system median accuracy of 89-100%, and adding folder information does not consistently improve predictions for files the rule misclassifies. Member nodes provide no consistent improvement over file-level graphs. These findings support assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide before attributing improvements to graph neural networks.

AI.tldr: On ten Java, C and C++ systems, dependency-aware file representations beat lexical ones and folder-aware HGT variants give the most consistent gains, yet a simple directory rule reaches 89% to 100% median per-system accuracy. The authors argue that what file representations and directory organization already provide should be assessed before crediting graph neural networks.
AI.motivation: Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture, but predictive gains alone do not show what additional graph processing contributes, since dependencies may already be encoded in the representations and directories may closely match the reference decomposition.
AI.method: The authors compare lexical, structural and contextual file representations with and without dependency neighbors under a limited labeling budget, using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer over file-level graphs extended with member nodes, folder nodes or both, plus a variant that encodes folder paths directly in file representations, and compare against a directory rule on the same labeled files.
AI.result: Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical ones on most systems, and neighbor aggregation can help depending on the predictor and direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains, but the directory rule achieves 89% to 100% per-system median accuracy, folder information does not consistently fix the files the rule misclassifies, and member nodes give no consistent improvement over file-level graphs.
AI.conclusion: Assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide should precede attributing improvements to graph neural networks in code-to-architecture mapping.

title: Co$^2$ODE: Conditionally Coarse-Grained Model Discovery for Rewiring in Biochemical Networks
summary: Biochemical networks propagate the signals that regulate cellular behaviour, and which routes carry them depends on cellular context: a shift in context rewires the network's effective dynamics. Mechanistic simulators are misspecified here because the effective dynamics emerge from an interaction structure that is only partially known. Model discovery instead learns the dynamics from data, but sparse, correlated measurements poorly identify a full network model. What matters is narrower: the portion the context rewires. We introduce conditionally coarse-grained ODEs (Co$^2$ODE), which model that portion as a sparse neural or symbolic ODE: a conditional mask selects the markers carrying the rewiring, and a variational autoencoder compresses the remaining markers into a learnt closure term. On single-cell phosphoproteomic data spanning 30 cancer-relevant overexpressions, Co$^2$ODE compresses a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while matching the predictive accuracy of a neural ODE fit to the full panel. The closure absorbs what the mask drops, hence the accuracy is insensitive to which markers are kept. Adding a prior score to the loss shifts the selected markers at no cost in fit, indicating the data are not interventional enough to identify the underlying biology.

AI.tldr: Co^2ODE models the context-rewired portion of a biochemical network as a sparse neural or symbolic ODE, with a conditional mask selecting the rewiring markers and a variational autoencoder compressing the rest into a closure term. On single-cell phosphoproteomic data across 30 cancer-relevant overexpressions it compresses a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while matching a neural ODE fit to the full panel.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic simulators are misspecified because the interaction structure is only partly known, and model discovery from sparse, correlated measurements poorly identifies a full network model, so the useful target is the portion that context rewires.
AI.method: A conditional mask selects the markers carrying the rewiring and models them as a sparse neural or symbolic ODE, while a variational autoencoder compresses the remaining markers into a learnt closure term.
AI.result: Co^2ODE compresses a 30-marker panel into a 10-dimensional state while matching the predictive accuracy of a neural ODE fit to the full panel. Accuracy is insensitive to which markers are kept because the closure absorbs what the mask drops, and adding a prior score to the loss shifts the selected markers at no cost in fit.
AI.conclusion: The data are not interventional enough to identify the underlying biology, so the selected markers are not uniquely determined, and the approach mainly yields a compact predictive model.

title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules
summary: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces three lightweight modules for medical lesion segmentation: a topology-aware loss, a 3D Group Prompt and a Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering organ and lesion segmentation are said to verify their efficacy.
AI.motivation: Rare pathologies lack high-quality annotations, which leads to morphological distortions despite seemingly ideal DSC scores, isolated development of individual segmentation tasks blocks shared knowledge, and constrained access to historical data triggers catastrophic forgetting when new classes are added.
AI.method: The DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling optimizes differentiable topological structure and boundary continuity; the 3D Group Prompt uses curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts and text prompts built on the SAT baseline to extract domain-universal knowledge; and a Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head with synonym-resolved routing replaces conventional output layers to enable incremental learning.
AI.result: The abstract reports ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering organ and lesion segmentation that verify the efficacy of the modules, with negligible added computational cost for the head; it gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The three modules offer a lightweight way to improve clinical applicability and to learn new categories incrementally without sacrificing performance on old tasks.

title: $\nabla$Mimic: Ultra-Efficient Humanoid Control with Differentiable Simulation
summary:
Robot policy learning is dominated by zeroth-order methods such as PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box and pay for it with enormous sample counts. First-order policy learning differentiates through the dynamics, but on contact-rich whole-body control it has rarely worked: its gradients explode. A recent world-model method showed that derivative information can make humanoid motion tracking far more efficient, using surrogate gradients of a learned model. We show that exact gradients of the simulator itself do better, once two obstacles are removed. Exact gradients contain rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges near some events; and they are expensive, because the simulator's adjoint has to replay the contact solve. $
abla$Mimic bounds these samples with median-relative per-sample gradient clipping at every step of the backward pass, and reuses each costly simulated window by multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets, which bounds every action target independently of the gradient scale. NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulation engine for the Unitree G1, removes the cost: it computes MuJoCo's full contact dynamics with fused per-world kernels and the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel, with analytic gradients that match float64 finite differences, $11.5	imes$ faster than the available MuJoCo Warp adjoint. On whole-body tracking of all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, $
abla$Mimic reaches the score reported by the state-of-the-art world-model method, 0.82, in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. SHAC, the standard first-order baseline, stops on exploding gradients within minutes. We release NablaEngine and $
abla$Mimic as open-source infrastructure for first-order humanoid policy learning.

AI.tldr: nabla-Mimic is a first-order humanoid control method that uses exact simulator gradients, stabilized by median-relative per-sample gradient clipping and multistep regression, together with NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulation engine for the Unitree G1. It reaches a 0.82 whole-body tracking score in 20 minutes, versus 1.2 hours for the state-of-the-art world-model method.
AI.motivation: Zeroth-order methods such as PPO are sample-hungry, and first-order methods through contact-rich whole-body dynamics have rarely worked because exact gradients contain rare unbounded samples where contact derivatives diverge and are expensive to compute through the simulator adjoint.
AI.method: Per-sample gradient clipping relative to the median is applied at every step of the backward pass, and each costly simulated window is reused through multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets that are bounded independently of gradient scale; NablaEngine computes MuJoCo's full contact dynamics with fused per-world kernels and the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel.
AI.result: On whole-body tracking of all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, nabla-Mimic reaches 0.82, the score of the state-of-the-art world-model method, in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 hours, and 0.874 in 1.8 hours, while SHAC stops on exploding gradients within minutes. NablaEngine's analytic gradients match float64 finite differences and run 11.5 times faster than the MuJoCo Warp adjoint.
AI.conclusion: With bounded gradient samples and a fast exact-gradient engine, first-order policy learning becomes practical for humanoid control, and the code and engine are released as open-source infrastructure.

title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory
summary: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: This survey organizes embodied memory along six memory requirements and eight architectural categories, analyzes their capabilities and limitations, and reviews how benchmarks distinguish genuine use of historical information from general task performance. It closes with open challenges in relevant-experience selection, belief consistency and cross-episode consolidation.
AI.motivation: Effective interaction with dynamic environments requires agents to act with partial knowledge and to retain, retrieve and update information from past observations, actions and experiences, which strong perception and reasoning alone do not provide.
AI.method: The survey uses two complementary dimensions: six memory requirements spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance and experiential learning, and eight architectural categories including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory and experience-based systems.
AI.result: The survey reports no experiments of its own; it analyzes the capabilities and limitations of existing approaches and examines how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior.
AI.conclusion: Memory is an essential component of reliable, adaptive and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence, and the proposed framework is offered as a way to understand it.

title: TSBPO: Tree-Structured Branching for Policy Optimization in Interactive Language Agents
summary: Training interactive language agents from terminal outcomes poses three coupled problems: which task and state continuations to sample, how to assign delayed feedback to decisions, and how to aggregate token losses for multi-token actions. We present TSBPO, a tree-structured sampling-to-update paradigm that addresses these problems within one training loop. A likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator uses retained task and state evidence to target continuations likely to produce contrasting terminal outcomes under fixed rollout budgets. On the resulting replayed physical trees, trajectory advantages compare immediate sibling segments, while observation-group step advantages compare outcomes at matched task/observation states. The actor then sums clipped token surrogates over each complete response and normalizes across active turns, avoiding response-length averaging in the policy-gradient term. With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, fixed checkpoints obtain 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and an 81.07% per-episode success rate over six stochastic episodes for each of the 500 WebShop test goals. A WebShop step-term ablation yields 75.93% at the same update-100 evaluation; an ALFWorld aggregation comparison shows higher observed command validity with complete-turn weighting. These results support the evaluated training configuration on two interactive benchmarks.

AI.tldr: TSBPO trains interactive language agents with a tree-structured sampling-to-update paradigm, reaching 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and 81.07% per-episode success on WebShop with a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor. Its gains are attributed to a Root/Branch allocator, sibling-based advantages and complete-response token aggregation.
AI.motivation: Training interactive language agents from delayed terminal outcomes poses three coupled problems: which task and state continuations to sample, how to assign delayed feedback to decisions, and how to aggregate token losses for multi-token actions.
AI.method: A likelihood-fitted Root/Branch allocator targets continuations likely to yield contrasting terminal outcomes under fixed rollout budgets; trajectory advantages compare immediate sibling segments and observation-group step advantages compare outcomes at matched task/observation states; the actor sums clipped token surrogates over each complete response and normalizes across active turns, avoiding response-length averaging in the policy-gradient term.
AI.result: With a Qwen2.5-1.5B actor, fixed checkpoints obtain 97.79% seen and 96.64% unseen stochastic success on ALFWorld and 81.07% per-episode success over six stochastic episodes for each of 500 WebShop test goals. A WebShop step-term ablation yields 75.93% at the same update-100 evaluation, and an ALFWorld aggregation comparison shows higher observed command validity with complete-turn weighting.
AI.conclusion: The evaluated training configuration performs well on two interactive benchmarks, supporting the value of tree-structured branching and complete-turn aggregation for policy optimization in language agents.

title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
summary: In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.

AI.tldr: The paper turns quantum measurement shot noise into a resource for diffusion sampling by using it in place of part of the noise a DDIM sampler injects, with a state-dependent adaptive shot budget. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture it reaches comparable generation quality with 303 shots per sample, against 1.6 million shots for a high-shot reference, about 5300 times fewer.
AI.motivation: Suppressing finite-shot readout noise in a quantum neural network requires repeated measurements that raise its cost, while stochastic diffusion samplers deliberately add randomness at each reverse step.
AI.method: Measurement error is modelled as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout, and the diffusion process is formulated on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex; compensation noise matches the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under minimum shot conditions, which yields a shot count that increases as the DDIM sampler becomes more deterministic.
AI.result: On the eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with 303 shots per sample against a high-shot reference of 1.6 million, about 5300 times fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.
AI.conclusion: Measurement randomness can replace part of a sampler's injected noise, which substantially reduces the shot cost of quantum diffusion generation, as shown on the Gaussian mixture and MNIST latent experiments.

title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: By re-running the official OLMo 2 1B mid-training stage with controlled document insertions, the study shows that one exposure raises a document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Matched-pair designs give a paired test 80% power to detect training on a collection, whereas document-level membership inference remains limited.
AI.motivation: Most membership-inference evaluations collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive, and a controlled setting is needed to separate training exposure from distribution differences.
AI.method: The authors re-ran the 50-billion-token mid-training stage of OLMo 2 1B, inserting one document from each of 7,814 domain- and difficulty-matched pairs chosen by coin flip, with the AI2 run from the same seed serving as the counterfactual reference, and compared reference-ratio attacks, paired tests and reference-free attacks.
AI.result: The reference ratio has an AUC of 0.767 but catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate with one threshold across domains. Thirteen matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains, and the full official post-training recipe leaves 89% of the average effect.
AI.conclusion: Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference, although collection-level detection is feasible with matched pairs.

title: Peeling the Matryoshka: Extracting Ontological Structure from Retrieval Embeddings
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 13 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Taxonomy construction is essential for knowledge-intensive NLP yet remains costly: clustering-based methods (i) need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines (ii) depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. We report an empirical finding that bears on both: in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, where each leading prefix is itself a usable, coarser vector, prefix length aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies; shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate the alignment to the learned early prefix dimensions. The pattern holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models. To test whether this regularity is usable, we introduce PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies): a minimal probe over these frozen embeddings, trained once with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment; a minimum spanning arborescence then decodes taxonomic DAGs. Using only a concept vocabulary (no documents), PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks, transferring to a new domain with no target-edge supervision. The end-to-end OLLM pipeline, which jointly discovers concepts and induces structure from document corpora, is reported as a cross-task reference. Pre-trained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient; a minimal probe renders it as explicit parent-child (is-a) structure.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that leading prefixes of Matryoshka Representation Learning embeddings align with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies, and proposes PEEL, a minimal order-embedding probe over frozen embeddings that decodes taxonomic DAGs from a concept vocabulary alone. PEEL transfers to a new domain without target-edge supervision.
AI.motivation: Taxonomy construction remains costly: clustering methods need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains.
AI.method: PEEL is a minimal probe trained once over frozen MRL embeddings with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment, and a minimum spanning arborescence decodes taxonomic DAGs from a concept vocabulary without documents.
AI.result: PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks and transfers to a new domain with no target-edge supervision, while the end-to-end OLLM pipeline is reported as a cross-task reference. The prefix alignment holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models, and shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate it to the learned early prefix dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient, and a minimal probe can render it as explicit parent-child (is-a) structure.
